subtopic: LEAVE TO MEMBERS OF PARLIAMENT ON ACTIVE SERVICE IN CANADA TO ATTEND SESSIONS

speechtext: On the orders of the day:

subtopic: LEAVE TO MEMBERS OF PARLIAMENT ON ACTIVE SERVICE IN CANADA TO ATTEND SESSIONS
speechtext:
I
should like to direct a question to the associate Minister of National Defence (Mr. Power):
1.	Has a regulation been issued by the Department of National Defence denying leave to members of parliament on active service in Canada who may desire to attend parliamentary sessions?
2.	Would the minister care to tell the house the nature and purpose of any such regulation and if a similar regulation is in operation in Great Britain?

speakeroldname: Hon. C. G. POWER (Associate Minister of National Defence):
speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
subtopic: LEAVE TO MEMBERS OF PARLIAMENT ON ACTIVE SERVICE IN CANADA TO ATTEND SESSIONS
speechtext:
My hon. friend was
good enough to give me notice of these questions.
If I may be permitted to speak for the senior service, there are no members of parliament in the navy. With respect to the air force, an order has been issued-not a regulation-to the effect that no special leave will be granted to members of parliament which will take them away from their train-

The Address-Mr. Hanson (York-Sunbury)
ing. It is however possible on request that members of parliament may obtain from two to four days for the purpose of attending parliament should that be necessary.
With regard to the army, there is an order, issued on January 23, addressed "To district officers commanding, all military districts":
Members of parliament and provincial legislatures appointed to active service units.
Leave of absence.
I am to inform you that such members of the federal parliament and provincial legislatures as may have been enrolled in units called out for .active service, will be permitted, so long as their units remain in Canada, if they so desire, to attend the sessions and be granted leave of absence without pay and allowances for the periods of such absence.
To sum up: With respect to the navy, at the moment no members of parliament are in the service. With respect to the air force, no special leave is granted to attend the sessions of parliament. With respect to the army, there is an old regulation to the effect that if they do attend the sessions of parliament they will do so without obtaining pay and allowance.
As regards the rest of the question, I am not familiar with the practice that obtains in Great Britain.

subtopic: PROCEEDING TO ORDER FOR RESUMING DEBATE ON ADDRESS

speakeroldname: Right Hon. W. L. MACKENZIE KING (Prime Minister):
speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: PROCEEDING TO ORDER FOR RESUMING DEBATE ON ADDRESS
speechtext: It was understood yesterday that we would not to-day resume the debate on the motion of the Minister of Finance (Mr. Usley) but would proceed with the special order and continue the debate on the address. If therefore the house is agreeable I shall ask that we proceed to that order.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY

speechtext: The house resumed from Monday, December 2, consideration of the motion of Mr. Brooke Claxton for an address to His Excellency the Governor General in reply to his speech at the opening of the session, and the amendment thereto of Mr. Hanson (York-Sunbury) and the amendment to the amendment of Mr. Blackmore.

speakeroldname: Hon. R. B. HANSON (Leader of the Opposition):
subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
I desire to detain the house for a brief period of time in order that I may sum up my impressions with respect to this protracted debate.
The debate proper started three weeks ago to-day, and we have listened to progress reports from eight ministers of the crown.
I had almost expected a ninth, because we were hoping to hear from the Minister of Pensions (Mr. Mackenzie) all last week. I think perhaps some word is due from him with respect to what is proposed to be done for men who went overseas with the Canadian active service force or those who did not go overseas and have now been discharged from the army. I understand they number about
15,000,	and men are being let out every day. They do constitute a real problem for Canada, for the government and for the communities in which they live. It would appear to me that a statement should be made by the Minister of Pensions and National Health as to the government policy. I understand that a policy has been laid down and is crystallized in a lengthy order in council, which I have endeavoured to study but which I think is not clearly understood by the country. Therefore if a convenient time could be arranged for a statement from the Minister of Pensions and National Health in this regard I think it would be of some importance.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: Will my hon. friend allow me to say that the Minister of Pensions and National Health has unfortunately suffered from an attack of flu during the past week and for that reason was prevented from being in the house. He was here yesterday and hoped to be able to speak. When he found he was not in shape for speaking he so informed me and intimated that he would speak to-day. I received word from the minister this morning that he did not think it would be possible for him to be in the house this afternoon. He hopes however to be able to make a statement before the week is out. If he himself is unable to do so, a statement will be made by one of the other ministers covering the subject raised.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
I quite
appreciate that, and that will be satisfactory-

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Order. I think the hon. leader of the opposition will appreciate what I am going to say. We have now before us a motion, an amendment and a subamendment. The leader of the opposition has already spoken on the main motion and moved his amendment. Citation No. 410 of Beauchesne reads:
Amendments to the address are moved by way of additions thereto. A general debate may take place on the address, but when an amendment is proposed the discussion should be strictly confined to the subject matter of the amendment.
I take it from the remarks the leader of the opposition has already made that he proposes to discuss the main motion and whatever may have subsequently come before the
606	COMMONS
The Address-Mr. Hanson (York-Sunbury)
house, but according to the citation I have quoted it is not in order at the present stage of the debate to discuss other than the terms of the subamendment. If I permit the leader of the opposition to engage in a general discussion in regard to all that has taken place I shall have to permit other hon. members of the house to do so, which would be contrary to the rules. Any other hon. member could take the same position and again discuss the main motion. I therefore desire to call the attention of the leader of the opposition to the rule and to point out that so far as relevancy is concerned any remarks at the present stage should be addressed solely to the subamendment.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Of course that was my intention, and my interpretation of the subamendment is that it is of very wide character and will allow very wide latitude.
I am glad to have the Prime Minister's undertaking that a statement will be made in connection with the important matter to which I have alluded.
The subamendment to which Mr. Speaker has so properly called my attention is so wide in its scope, having to do with the financing of the war and the general attitude thereto, that I am fully conscious that I am within my right in discussing what contributions have been made to the debate by ministers on previous occasions, and my remarks will largely be confined thereto.
Speaking in this debate prior to the moving of the subamendment I asked the government to give to the people of Canada a clear, truthful, factual and honest statement, free from propaganda and partisanship, so that we might examine it and know the nature and extent of Canada's war effort. I am asking myself to-day, and I ask hon. members of this house who have listened to those reports in the intervening days, how far they measure up to the requirements, judged by the standard to which I have alluded. I am bound to say that I personally listened to them with mixed feelings, and, may I say, with a sense of frustration and futility. And I am of opinion that this feeling must have been present in the minds of a large number of supporters of the government who have taken part in this debate, because we have listened from time to time to private members in this house supporting the administration who have given evidence not only of their desire to assist the government in its war effort, but of the absolute lack of facility and opportunity to make a contribution.
Many of the statements made by the ministers were factual; many were not. In my view there was less evidence of propa-

ganda intended to bolster up the government's position than in the statements to which we listened in the month of July last. For that I am truly grateful.
But still there is discernible most subtle evidence of propaganda, and that I believe is the effect on the mind of the public. There was throughout, with the possible exception of one address, a total failure to adopt and promote a more realistic attitude towards the war. May I at this juncture-

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: Would the hon. gentleman be kind enough to define what he means by "a more realistic attitude towards the war"?

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
I am
afraid I could not explain it to the hon. member, and I do not think I shall take the time of the house to make the attempt.
May I at this juncture refer to an address delivered last night in the city of Toronto by the premier of Ontario, in which he made a plea for a more realistic war attitude on the part of this government, and in which he turned his guns on a tight little group turning out propaganda in Ottawa. In that address he referred to the fact that Canadians have been told by the press agents of the government that an all-Canadian squadron flying all-Canadian Spitfires was organized and fighting in England. He went on to say:
Not one of these pilots had been trained as Canadian flyers. Many of them went over there after we turned down the empire training scheme. They paid their way over or worked their way over and were trained by the Royal Air Force.
It is to this type of propaganda that we have to read or listen to that I take objection. It is not factual.
May I here pause to remind the house and the country that on September 4 last the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Ralston) in opening the campaign for the second war loan, referred with great pride to the fact that a squadron of flyers on the other side had flown Hurricane planes made in Canada by Canadian working men in Canadian factories. To me that was an astonishing statement, because I had not understood that anything of the sort had been attempted in Canada. I had been following this question of aeroplane construction in Canada for some months and I knew that the most we could claim was that these Hurricanes had been assembled in Canada, but that the major parts had been made elsewhere. Now it is that kind of propaganda that in my view is calculated to lull the Canadian people into a false sense of security as to our war effort. And I leave with members of this house and with the country the thought that we should

The Address-Mr. Hanson (York-Sunbury)
not be fed with statements of that kind, which are not factual and are not based on the naked truth.
I believe the lack of realism on the part of the government's war effort was in a measure corrected yesterday when the Minister of Finance (Mr. Ilsley) brought down his first budget of the session. A careful perusal of his remarks and of the resolutions which he proposed, portions of which in my view were long overdue, will bring to the Canadian people a realization of what I have long visualized as necessary.
It will be recalled that as long ago as last July, after the fall of France, I called upon the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) to declare a state of national emergency in Canada. My theory then was that we would have to shock the Canadian people into a realization of the seriousness of the situation. What did we get? We got the national registration, and we got the mobilization act. The first measure has been used as a basis for the improvised thirty-day training scheme. But has it been used in connection with the mobilization of labour? Has it been used in connection with the mobilization of the material assets of this country? If so I suggest to you, Mr. Speaker, that there is absolutely no evidence of any such use having been made of it. And with respect to the thirty-day training plan and the mobilization act itself, was that anything more than an improvisation to ward off attacks on the government? Was it more than a half-way measure, the importance and value of which only time will tell? I suggest that it was only this.
I shall not pursue at this time the theme of yesterday's budget, except to say that in my view the government has announced some measures which should have been put into effect some time ago. In some respects it has not gone far enough, and I submit that there are serious omissions. Our exchange position is serious, I think much more serious than the Minister of Finance intimated to the country yesterday, and perhaps he was wise in not telling the whole story. He must have information that is denied to me, but I do say to the house and to the country that I have sufficient information at my command to lead me to think that the situation is serious, and that if we are to maintain anything like the present equilibrium we shall have to go far beyond the $60,000,000 or $70,000,000 which was indicated as the objective of yesterday's budget.
May I now attempt a brief review of the statements made by the various ministers, dealing first wfith that of the Prime Minister.
In his prepared speech delivered on November 12, instead of giving the Canadian people
factual information as to a concerted war effort the Prime Minister took an hour and a half to tell the Canadian people his views on the international situation as it had developed in the last few months. It was all very interesting, but I submit that it was not what the Canadian people were looking for. They are intelligent; they know for themselves what is the international situation. We did not expect the Prime Minister to deliver a review of the recent history of European developments or international developments; rather were we asking for a factual statement in a concrete way as to what he and his government were doing to help win the war. Because of that many of us were disappointed; and after reading newspaper comment from one end of the country to the other I believe the Canadian people were disappointed.
In my view, however, there was one outstanding omission from the Prime Minister's review of international affairs, having regard to the declarations contained in the speech from the throne and subsequent declarations. I ask him now: What, if any, are the commitments of this country to the United States qua Ogdensburg?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: None.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: All right; that is a very good answer. There are no commitments, and I am perfectly satisfied with that. But if there were commitments we ought to be told what they are. In the course of his remarks the Prime Minister took to himself great credit-and I do not deny it to him -for having built up a spirit of friendship with the United States.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: Hear, hear.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: Well, Mr. Speaker, he is entitled to that; I do not for a moment deny it. I will go further and say that it is of the very greatest importance at this time, and I said so at Toronto. I said at Toronto that the Ogdensburg conversations were capable of a great and noble purpose, and I have never said anything that would contravene that statement. We have no commitments; that is the statement made to-day. Well, I am not for a moment questioning the Prime Minister's word, but I am rather curious. I should like to bring to the attention of this house and of the country the fact that the Prime Minister's coadjutor- that may not be the proper word-his confidential secretary, the talented Mr. Brocking-ton, recently made a speech before the American Bar Association at Philadelphia.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Good speech.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: It was a grand speech; I wish I could make so eloquent a speech. As a pure piece of eloquence it was in a class by itself, and I told him so. speechtext: I have Mr. Brockington's letter. I am not going to read it to the house, but in it Mr. Brockington told me he was not authorized to make the statement. But he was very close to the Prime Minister, and I wondered why he made it if there were no basis for it.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Anyone who
is close to me is not, I trust, deprived of his right to say what he wishes or to draw inferences of his own, and I must not be held responsible for every word that is uttered by those who may be close to me.

speechtext:
I agree
with what the Prime Minister says, and Mr. Brockington was speaking on his own. If it is too strong a statement to say that he had dined too well, I cheerfully withdraw it; but that statement was made by Mr. Brockington; it received wide publicity both here and in the United States, and the general public concluded that there was a pact. Now the Prime Minister's statement to-day washes that all out, and I am content to leave the matter where it is.
Then may I ask the Prime Minister one further question in this regard. Has any report been made by the joint committee?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: Yes; several.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Several
reports have been made. Are we to be provided with copies of those reports, or are they considered to be confidential?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: As my hon. friend knows, those reports relate to matters which affect the security of this continent. They could not be made public without the consent of the government of the United States as well as the consent of our own government. Speaking for Canada I would say that as they relate to the defence of Canada and disclose information which would be of service to the enemy, they will not be made public.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Very
well. I find no fault with that attitude. I simply sought to know the facts: had a report been made. Now we are apprised of the fact that several reports have been made, and we can well leave the matter there.
The second minister to address the house was the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner). I may say I listened with interest to his story of his trip to England, to his report on the arrangements he had made for the purchase by Great Britain of bacon and other supplies, and to his prognostications on wheat. Later on I had the good fortune to listen to his radio address and his observations with regard to skilled labour in Canada, and the necessity for training men for warfare as opposed to training men for essential industry. That is a matter with which I shall deal later.
I have just this to say with respect to the bacon agreement. Three times I have asked to have this agreement tabled. Twice we have been put off. No one is competent to speak with respect to this agreement unless he has seen it, read it and digested it. I cannot do so, for that reason. But it seems to me that two or three facts emerge. First of all, England is to take larger quantities at lower prices. There are to be smaller Wiltshire sides and more pigs for less money. Is that a fair deduction?

speakerposition: Minister of National War Services; Minister of Agriculture
subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: No, not quite.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: I should like to refer to the effect the agreement has had on the bacon producers of eastern Canada. The question of mill feeds is of major importance to them in their bacon production. I have been told, and we all know it is a fact, that mill feeds have increased in price steadily during the past few months. The reason assigned is greater demand for mill feeds in the United States. Well, Mr. Speaker, I contend that the price of mill feeds has gone so high, having regard to transportation costs, that in eastern Canada our bacon producers cannot afford to buy mill feeds to finish their hogs.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
How do you know?

The Address-Mr. Hanson (York-Sunbury)

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
How do I know?-because I keep in touch with the people in that industry, and I get my information from sources similar to those from which the hon. member could get it, if he were to put his ear to the ground, or were to make intelligent inquiries. I am told in my province that with the price of mill feeds as high as it is to-day they cannot produce bacon for the price offered.
I am not suggesting that England should offer a higher price. That is their business. But I do suggest to the government that because the farmer in eastern Canada cannot produce at the present cost of mill feeds, something should be done for him. I understand that recently an order has gone out pegging the price of mill feeds. Well, better late than never; but I say it should have been done before. Our millers are not now suffering from the processing tax.
Nevertheless I am among those who do not think that we should exact the last cent from Britain. I do not think that Canada as a nation should become rich at the expense of our distressed brethren across the seas. On the contrary I say we should not haggle with England over prices of foodstuffs-and bacon is fourth in their list of necessities. Because of the other conditions to which I have referred, the farmer is producing below the cost of production. And I do suggest to the government that something ought to be done to assist the bacon farmers in this country. Just what the measure of that assistance should be I am not in a position to advise. I am not a technical agriculturist, and the Minister of Agriculture is. But I invite him to give consideration to the plight of the bacon producers in eastern Canada, with a view to seeing at least that they may get back a new dollar for an old one.
I am bound to tell this house that from information which I have from the other side of the water there is a feeling in England that Canada is seeking to make money out of the war.

I suggest we ought to do something to dissipate in England the feeling to which I have alluded, on the assumption that it exists.
I should like to refer only briefly to what the Minister of Agriculture had to say about wheat. He made a prophecy, and it was highly optimistic. I have seen certain reviews from western Canada with respect to that prophecy. There was one statement made by the premier of Manitoba. There is a review issued by the Sanford Evans statistical bureau, and also reviews from other well-informed

The Address-Mr. Hanson (York-Sunbury)
sources. I had intended to go into those reviews at greater length, but I shall content myself by referring only to the Sanford Evans statistical service, in which the minister's proposals and prophecies are analysed. All I can say is that it is based on the assumption that we shall consume more in Canada than we ever consumed in any single year of our history, that England will take more wheat than she ever took in any single year of her history, and that continental Europe, which is now overrun by the nazis, will in the days to come, and with the five-year plan, take more wheat than they have ever taken before.
The whole wheat speech of the Minister of Agriculture is part and parcel of the policy of the government to soothe the people of Canada, and especially the people of western Canada, into a false sense of security concerning the future of wheat in Canada.
I should like to refer briefly to the minister's broadcast on Sunday night, November 17. I enjoyed that broadcast. I pay him the compliment of saying that I have reread it. With a large portion of it I am entirely in agreement. It sounded a high note. Near the end of his speceh he said this:
I think it would be wise to stop much of this talk against military training for men who are making planes, munitions, arms and ships.
And further on he stated:
Factory managers who contend they cannot produce to capacity without interfering with the training of their men may have to be told by someone . . . that they . . . are not good enough for war time.
That was a threat to industry in Canada. I want to contrast that statement with a statement made during this debate, on Friday, November 15, by the Minister of National Defence, when he said:
I have said it before, and I say it again, that under present conditions it is essential to the completion of equipment and the completion of training of those large numbers of men we now have in the Canadian army, that the needs of war industry for man-power be not interfered with.
Here we have two members of the same cabinet, speaking in the same week from the same benches.

It is
immaterial. The fact is that the minister did make the statement, and thereby made a direct attack upon Canadian industry based on one isolated case. I say to you, Mr. Speaker, to the house and to the country that this is a most unfair position for the minister to take in connection with Canadian industry. I recall distinctly and clearly at the time of the outbreak of the war that Canadian industry came to this government and offered to cooperate to the full extent of its resources. I make the further statement that the government was slow in indicating a willingness to

The Address-Mr. Hanson (York-Sunbury)
accept this cooperation, but industry in Canada has loyally assumed the great tasks imposed upon it by the circumstances which have arisen, and is fulfilling those tasks with the utmost efficiency. Industry has been told that it must not and cannot make big profits, and it is an astonishing thing that Canadian industry should have been subjected to an attack by the Minister of National War Services.
I suggest to you, Mr. Speaker, and to the members of this house, that these diametrically opposed positions indicate that the government went about the business of making war without having anything like a comprehensive plan of cooperation. It is because there is no such plan that there is no real coordination, that ministers like the Minister of National War Services adopt one attitude and the Minister of National Defence adopts another.
May I turn briefly to the statement of the Minister of National Defence. We are all delighted to know that he has arrived safely in England, and I look forward with a great deal of confidence to his return with a coordinated plan, the result of the interchange of views with the British war ministry. I am sure that as a result of his visit there will be coordination between Canada's and Britain's war efforts. I know the Minister of National Defence and I feel quite sure that he would not go over there unless he wanted to know and do what was best in the common effort.
I listened to the minister's report with a great deal of interest. To a large degree it was factual, but it left many things to be desired.
May I pause here to say something which perhaps I should have said on November 12. It will be recalled that in his speech before the Canadian club at Ottawa Major-General Crerar indicated that the period of training was limited to thirty days because, for one reason, and aside altogether from the question of lack of equipment, it was desired to inculcate a sense of national obligation into a part of our young nationals. That was probably true to a degree in some parts of Canada, but not in every part. Our young men had a sense of national obligation in a very large measure, but they found that there was no outlet for that sense of national obligation. That theory was borne out by the announcement of a change of policy by the Minister of National Defence for Air. During this very debate he stated that hereafter the department over which he had the honour to preside would go out looking for airmen, rather than having airmen come

looking for them. I thought that was all to the good, and I applauded that change in policy.
I believe there is no lack of a sense of national obligation on the part of our young nationals. I put this question to the house: why should there be a lack of a sense of national obligation on the part of our young nationals in many parts of Canada? Is it that they have not been properly taught during the last twenty-five years to have a. sense of obligation? I do not know. I am asking the question. I am wondering if it is because of bad leadership or false leadership, in the past.

I regret I was not in the house when the Minister of National Defence for Naval Services (Mr. Macdonald) made his speech. I have read it since. It was moderate. I am one of those who think that the Royal Canadian Navy has been doing good work with very limited means and equipment.
According to the minister we are to embark on a shipbuilding plan. It is said that we are to build destroyers and perhaps cruisers. Well, I think we are a little late in starting. It will be a long time before we are able to make any distinct contribution to the winning of the war with Canadian-built naval vessels. It is true that we built some mine sweepers and some coastal vessels, but, aside from assisting in convoys, our contribution has been meagre indeed.
And now shall I read to you what Mr. Hepburn says about it-or shall I leave it to
your imagination? No, I do not intend to read it. Hon. gentlemen have all read it and it is none too complimentary.
All Canadians, I believe, will be pleased to learn that the government has decided to reopen the naval college, thereby rectifying a mistake that was made by the government of my right hon. friend almost twenty years ago when they closed the college. We thus deprived our young Canadians who were looking forward to a naval career of having a college in Canada to attend. They had to go abroad. One fine young naval cadet in my own county went to England at the expense of his parents and entered a naval college there. Last spring I had the pleasure of announcing, through the courtesy of the Deputy Minister of Naval Services in this country, that he had in the whole field of cadets won the King's Dirk, but he had to go to England to acquire that honour.
The minister indicated that it was the policy of the government to build in the near future destroyers in Canadian yards. He stated, in my opinion very rightly, that we did not have the necessary experts here, and therefore he had communicated with the authorities in Great Britain to ascertain if they could furnish the necessary experts in naval construction.
I am at a loss to understand how the minister can expect to get these experts from England when one considers that in this great war every shipyard in England is driving at top speed not only in naval construction but also in the building of merchant cargo ships. Furthermore, all the naval guns and necessary armaments would have to be imported from England, and they surely are not procurable now. That is a pity, but I believe I am stating a fact when I say that we cannot hope to get any substantial number of naval experts to come to Canada and help us in this shipbuilding programme. I may be wrong; the minister may have other information; but it would seem to me that these men would not be procurable at this time.
There is another obstacle in the way, which I think it is my duty to point out to the minister, and that is that the cost of naval construction, either in war or in peace time, would be so excessive as compared with construction in the United Kingdom that for economy's sake we ought to consider whether we should not have these ships built in England. This question came up very acutely in the late twenties. The Lady boats were built in England because it was understood and agreed by the government of the day, and by all parties who took any intelligent interest in the matter, that it would cost at
614	COMMONS
The Address-Mr. Hanson (York-Sunbury)
least fifty per cent more to build them in Canada. That consideration still obtains. However, I suppose we shall have to consider the question of building steel ships in this country, sooner perhaps than we think. The necessity is there and it may be that even if we have to pay a higher price it would be good national policy to do so.
The minister quite rightly states that Canada ought to have a stronger and more efficient navy. Hence his reason for advocating a policy of construction of destroyers in Canada. I am not an authority on naval matters, neither is the minister, so far as I know. He has to take expert advice. I should like however to quote to him one of the greatest authorities the world has known-the late Admiral Sir John Jellieoe. When Sir John Jellicoe visited Canada in connection with naval matters in 1920, the minimum policy he recommended for Canada was to provide immediately for three light cruisers, six destroyers and four submarines. We have at the present time twelve destroyers, and I am sure the minister will recognize that when he is considering a permanent policy it is not destroyers that we need but light cruisers and submarines and other craft. These light cruisers are armed with four 6-inch guns, antiaircraft guns and torpedo tubes. We all recall with a thrill of pride that it was three light cruisers of this type that defeated the German pocket battleship Graf Spee last December.
Destroyers are all right for a short distance when escorting convoys, but for proper protection a convoy must be protected by light cruisers; I think that is the experience of this war. Since this war began our convoys have very often been escorted not only by light cruisers but even by battleships.
There is one other matter to which I should like to allude in a discussion of our navy. I am sure we all appreciate the great responsibility that rests upon the shoulders of the minister as well as the director of naval service to see that no officers shall be appointed as destroyer commanders or to other senior posts unless they are fully qualified. To state that is to state a truism. No better naval officers exist in the world than Canadians when properly trained. Our merchant marine men indicate that. But a naval career, according to the best British standards, requires not only graduation from a naval college but long years of training afloat, first as midshipman, then sub-lieutenant and then lieutenant; and many years elapse before anyone can expect to be promoted to the rank of captain.
The late Lord Jellicoe stated, when he was in Canada on his naval mission, that it takes

nine years to make a good lieutenant gunner. I realize that when our naval service now have twelve destroyers, they must be sore pressed for officers, more especially for the senior commands, and I have confidence enough in both the minister and his officers to believe that they would not appoint Canadians to important senior commands unless they were fully qualified.

I have not suggested that there was anything but unfortunate circumstances whereby these ships were lost. I did not know the late Commander Roy, but the house may be interested to know that his wife was, I think, a native of my city; at all events her grandfather lived there and was a distinguished member of the other chamber during his lifetime.
I want to devote a few minutes to the Minister of Munitions and Supply (Mr. Howe). We heard from him and got a wealth of information with regard to contracts let and commitments made; but we got nothing with respect to production and deliveries. The Prime Minister should tell the house and the country plainly what the

The Address-Mr. Hanson (York-Sunbury)
attitude of the government is with respect to this important matter. Are we or are we not to have information with respect to production and delivery? It may be that it is not in the public interest that this information should be given; if that is so it ought to be made quite clear to the house and the country, and the reasons given for the refusal.
One further thing, at the risk of returning to a prosaic matter, which the Associate Minister of National Defence called a " slimy " matter-are we to have unit prices?
I think the country will demand that. So far as I am concerned, unless I am shown that it is absolutely in the public interest that we should not have unit prices, I shall continue to press for them.
Speaking on a former occasion I requested specifically that parliament be informed as to what results had been attained with respect to production and deliveries, because we held the view, and I believe it is well founded, that it was the deliberate policy of the government, during the past session as well as during the interval since we adjourned in August, to endeavour to create, by general statements of what we are going to do in the future, the impression that all was well with our war effort in the way of production and deliveries. And if there is any doubt of that I will page Mr. Hepburn and see what he says about it. It was our view that the government has sought to lull and soothe the Canadian people into a false sense of security, and continues to do so. We believe that there is a danger behind such a position. Hence the amendment which I have had the honour to move in this house.
Therefore I felt impelled to ask the government that it cause to be set up immediately two select special committees, charged with the responsibility and the duty of investigating and reporting to this house, factually, objectively and truthfully, without bias and without partisanship, what our exact position is to-day (a) with respect to our fighting forces, military, naval and air, and (b) with respect to the production and delivery of all the important materials, equipment and supplies necessary to our war effort, so that the Canadian people might know the truth.
So far, such committees have not been set up. I indicated that I knew there were difficulties, and I would ask the Prime Minister, if he can and will, to tell the house what the attitude of the government is with respect to that. If the difficulties are such as cannot be surmounted then I have another concrete suggestion which I desire to lay before the house and the country. It is, in brief, that the government cause to be set up a select committee
on current expenditure defrayed out of moneys provided by parliament for the defence services, for civil defence and for other services directly connected with the war, and instruct such committee to report what, if any, economies consistent with the execution of government policies may be effected therein.
Now, it is all very well to say that we can get all this information on national expenditure through the public accounts committee. Theoretically that is correct. But the information which will be obtained through the public accounts idea will not be on current expenditure. It will relate only to the expenditures that have taken place in the previous year and as covered by the auditor general's report. Practically all the national expenditure for the war effort has taken place since March 31 last -or rather the great bulk of the contracts relating to national expenditure for war effort have been let since March 31, and inquiry before the public accounts committee will not be possible. That committee may _ examine only such things as are submitted to it. I am impelled to make this request for various reasons, hut more particularly because what I suggest has been done in England and, I am advised, with good results.
I hold in my hand a series of reports of a select standing committee of the British parliament which was set up under the authority of an order of reference made on December 12, 1939, while Mr. Chamberlain was still Prime Minister and while there was an official opposition. The order of reference contains this:
That a select committee be appointed to examine the current expenditure defrayed out of moneys provided by parliament for the defence services, for civil defence and for otheT services directly connected with the war, and to report what, if any, economies consistent with the execution of the policy decided by the government may be effected therein.
Then it goes on and appoints a committee of twenty-eight members-and not one of them is a member of the government; they are all private members, and so far as I read the list of names, none of them is of international prominence. The committee has the usual power to send for persons, papers and records, and to sit notwithstanding any adjournment of the house, and to adjourn from place to place. It was to be in effect a continuous working committee to examine current expenditures for war purposes having regard to the announced policy of the government. It had the power to appoint subcommittees and to refer to such subcommittees any of the matters within the jurisdiction of the committee. Such subcommittees so appointed were empowered to send for persons, papers and records, to sit notwithstanding any adjournment of the house,

and to adjourn from place to place. This select committee has been sitting almost constantly since it iwas set up. Its first report was made in January, and the last I have was made on August 21, 1940. Any hon. gentleman who peruses this report will see, I am sure, that it is serving a great national purpose-not in opposition to government policy, not to the detriment of government policy, but to assist government policy, and to see what if any economies can be attained by suggestions.
My view is that we ought to have something like that here in Canada. It is a way in which private members could contribute to the war effort. I have heard dozens of members who support the government bewail the fact that they could not do anything to help, and saying that private members ought to be in a position to do something to help.
So far the war effort of the government has been carried out on the line of a closed corporation, so far as members of parliament are concerned. I submit this to the government as a constructive proposal to which they should give some attention. I submit it in the utmost good faith, not by way of criticism but by way of being helpful to the government. We know that war is wasteful; we know there is great waste in this war, though I do not say intentional waste. I do believe, however, that a committee of private members of this house, sitting day in and day out during sessions and between sessions, could perform a very useful function in assisting the government at this time, and I commend this suggestion to hon. members. It will provide an outlet for the energies of the private members who are anxious about the war, who want to make a contribution, who were sent here by their constituents to make that contribution but who find themselves frustrated-yes, that is the word-because they have no outlet for their abilities and their capabilities.
I do hope that the Prime Minister will accept this suggestion, and before I leave the topic may I say to hon. gentlemen who will accept positions on the committee, if it be set up:	There is not only a real job to be
done, but a job which will tax your capabilities to the utmost. You will have to make substantial sacrifices in serving the state in this way, but it is a patriotic duty which I think some of you ought to perform. I believe a real contribution can be made in this way by private members.
Now I should like to make some little reference to the Minister of Finance (Mr. Ilsley), and I shall endeavour to keep away from the question of foreign exchange, which has become a major topic to be dealt with at another time.

I thought it was just what one would expect from the financial mentors of the minister. When I say that my hon. friends to my left can take it from me that I am in agreement with orthodox finance for war purposes.

I do not wish out of hand to condemn the professional bond and investment dealers. They serve a very useful purpose in connection with war loans. They can get the big subscriptions, but I suggest to you, Mr. Speaker, and to hon. members of this house that they cannot get the individual investors interested in these loans. Therefore I congratulate the minister upon his change of heart in having accepted what I considered to be a constructive suggestion.
I criticized the last budget because of its income tax proposals with respect to individual taxpayers. I said then and I say now that there was no equality of sacrifice there. The well-disposed were unduly taxed, and the tax was thrust upon them with great suddenness and severity. The minister fell into what I considered a curious error when he interpreted my words "the well-disposed" to mean "the well-to-do." In my view the two terms are not synonymous; the well-disposed may not necessarily be the well-to-do. The minister comes from an old evangelical religious body. Has he never heard of the widow's mite? I am sure he has. I use that as an illustration to point out the error into which I think he has fallen.

to the war savings certificates. That is good; publicity is necessary and desirable, but we have to do something more. Yesterday I had a letter from a gentleman in the city of Saint John who is in charge of this work in the province of New Brunswick, one of the finest citizens of Canada, who will give voluntarily his service, his time and his private means to help put this over. He deplores the fact that the public has not responded; and that is the case, since we are not getting $2,000,000 a month from this source. Just what is the cure I do not know. There will have to be concerted action. In my own community the gentleman who has charge of this campaign tells me that he is all but throwing up his hands because of the lack of sympathy for this movement, even in that community.
We must do something to ensure the success of this campaign. If we are to attain the objective of $10,000,000 a month in war savings certificates some people will have to bestir themselves. I do beseech the members of this house to take action. Each is a leader of public opinion in his own community; that was indicated by the work done by the members in putting over the national registration. Let every one of us get behind the sale of these war savings certificates, for the honour of our own communities. Let us see if we cannot help the government put this thing over. It is a patriotic duty and one which I think every one of us ought to assume on his own account.
Now I should like to say just a word about the Minister of Labour (Mr. McLarty), to whose address I listened with a good deal of interest. The impression he left on my mind was that he was flying a kite to labour. He would have labour depart from its present standards for the duration of the war. I do not know what will be the response of labour. I believe it will be a patriotic response, but I think it will have to be made abundantly clear to labour that if it is to give up its present standards it shall be for the duration and for the duration only. Then I am sure labour will respond as it has responded in England.
I have just a word to say with regard to parliament adjourning until February 17. In my view the adjournment will be too long, but the Prime Minister has explained that in the view of the government it is necessary to take this long adjournment. I am glad to know, however, that it is upon the distinct understanding that should certain eventualities materialize, such as were outlined in the Prime Minister's statement of August 3 last,
in connection with the motion presented on that day, we will be called together sooner, and with that I am content.
I have been impressed, Mr. Speaker, by the appeal that has been made by private members of this house during the course of this debate, and particularly by members supporting the administration, that more use should be made of private members and of the standing committees of the house. There is, as I gather, a feeling of manifest uneasiness, a sense of frustration at the lack of functioning on the part of parliament itself. Well, I suggest to hon. gentlemen that this is true, and the fault is the government's, because the government has taken authority to do everything parliament used to do. That may be necessary in war time, but I do suggest that to a large degree we have abdicated our functions and that there has been too much delegation of power. There is manifest in the house a will to do on the part of the elected representatives of the people, and a complete failure in performance because of lack of opportunity. The government are carrying on the war effort, as it were, as a closed corporation, and hon. members are not satisfied.
But we of this party shall not falter. We shall, as opportunity offers, cooperate with the government along the general lines indicated when I spoke on November 12, and we shall do our best to get the results so urgently needed.
In passing may I refer to the observations of the hon. member for Victoria B.C. (Mr. Mayhew) who indicated that in his view my rededication of this party to the service of the state at this time was the highlight of my address of three weeks ago. He indicated, however, regret that I myself did not lay down a policy for a war effort. Well, I do not conceive that at this juncture it is my function or within my power to do that. Why do I say this? I say it for the obvious reason that no one can enunciate a policy unless he is briefed with the facts upon which to base a policy. The facts are not accessible to us-in fact they are denied to us.
Having regard to all the statements made by the ministers with regard to the government's war effort, certain things emerge. First, we have been served with reports similar in most respects to the progress reports which we heard last summer. I am bound to repeat that there is not as much propaganda in what we have listened to during these past three weeks as there was in the reports heard last summer, but their general tenor and purport is the same.

618	COMMONS
The Address-Mr. Hanson (York-Sunbury)
The second point which emerges is that there is abundant evidence that the government lacks a real war programme of production. Apparently the government has become seized of that position, because recently, as late as November 16, order in council 6601 was passed, setting up the war-time requirements board, under the chairmanship of an able business executive, Mr. H. R. MacMillan, and with a retinue of departmental officials. The whole success of this war-time requirements board will centre around the chairman. He is to become the "Sir Joseph" of the effort of the government. Whatever may have been said about the other "Sir Joseph", I say that he was the greatest business man of his time in Canada, and that he did wonderful work for the imperial munitions board. Mr. MacMillan is a capable man, and I wish him well.
Let us for a moment analyse the position with respect to this war-time requirements board. Section 2 of the order in council sets out the powers of the board, and I submit to the Prime Minister that they are entirely inadequate if the board is to do the maximum work it ought to do under this authority. Subsection (a) of that section provides for the securing of information; (b) provides for the coordination and analysis of such information; (c) provides for the formulation of such plans as may be necessary to ensure that war needs in order of importance shall have priority over all other needs. That is all to the good. There must be someone to say what shall have priority. Then, subsection
(d)	provides that the Department of Munitions and Supply and the controllers and divisions thereof, and any other departments of the government shall be kept informed by the war-time requirements board upon the matters previously referred to, such as production, the use of materials, manufacturing plants and facilities, transportation facilities, and the obtaining of statements of prospective needs of the fighting services.
The criticism I make-and it is a constructive criticism-is that the board has not sufficient power, and that everything must be referred back to the Minister of Munitions and Supply, who still keeps control. I am serious in that criticism. That, I believe, is the weakness of the board. I am certain, however, that if he finds his efforts under the order in council thwarted by the lack of power, the chairman will apply for additional powers and get them, or know the reason why.
Looking over the whole picture it is quite apparent that in six months time the attitude of the government has undergone a marked
!Mr. R. B. Hanson.]
change in outlook. In May last the government had assumed a complacent attitude. That was certainly the feeling in the country and in the house; and if hon. members do not believe me I suggest that -they go back and read the speech of the hon. member for Vancouver North (Mr. Sinclair) in moving the address in reply at that time.
Then came the tragic trend of events in May and late June, the invasion of Norway, the fall of the low countries, and finally the fall of France and the epic of Dunkirk. Then, shocked by all this, we witnessed a series of hasty improvisations. What was the mobilization act? It was a hasty improvisation to ward off an attack on the government's war effort-or lack of effort. But the declarations at that time gave no possible evidence of a real war programme, and down to date we have not been told of a definite war programme. It is true that the staff officers have evolved a plan for the defence of Canada, whatever it is-but we are not told what it is. I do not think we Shall be.
We are told by the Prime Minister that during all the years that he attended imperial conferences it was laid down as a fundamental that the dominions were to take care of home defence. I can well believe that, because neither he nor anyone in his entourage at that time would ever consider doing anything else, and never at any time admitted any obligation to the principle of empire defence. Since the war all these preconceived ideas have gone by the board, and to-day, fifteen months after war started, the government is giving support to the theory of empire defence, notwithstanding what some of its supporters are saying in the country.
The difference between the Prime Minister and myself is that I want Canada to go ahead on a well-defined war effort, based upon our willingness and capabilities, and in conformity with empire requirements in the theatre of war, while he pursued, up to a certain point, a course based on a -theory of providing for our own defence first-in Canada. I am glad to think that force of public criticism and the tragic trend of events has, to a degree, reversed the situation. This, to me, is satisfactory, so far as it goes.
I have been told, and it stands to reason, that the greatest effort of a country situated as Canada is-an acknowledged belligerent- should be based on the theory that we should contribute to the utmost toward the winning of the war in the actual theatre of war-not here in Canada three thousand miles removed from the actual theatre of war, where our only effort would be required to repel invasion, and then only after the battle had been lost overseas.

The Address-Mr. Coldwell
That is the advice that was given to the Prime Minister by a great soldier in Canada. I am pleased to think that in some degree the Prime Minister has come around to that way of thinking. In so far as he has done so he is, I think, to be commended.
I shall detain the house only a moment longer to say that I was disturbed by the Prime Minister's speech of yesterday. I do not believe he did justice to himself, and certainly he did less than justice to me. On Thursday last I spoke about my impressions with regard to the war situation. I spoke about the seriousness of that situation and, knowing of the Prime Minister's greater knowledge of what was taking place, I asked him to give the house a review of the position. At that time, in addition to stressing the seriousness of the situation, I asked him to indicate what, if anything, Canada could do at this juncture toward giving further aid and assistance, whether by way of men, materials, supplies or equipment.
On that occasion the Prime Minister stated he had had in mind making a statement to the house respecting the situation. He said, among other things:
I agree with my hon. friend in his view that the situation is a serious one. I think anyone reading the press would gather that opinion. I would also say that such information as the government itself is receiving the press would appear to be reflecting accurately. Any statement that I may have to make will be practically in accord with what has already appeared in the press.
I was happy at that reply. I thought it was an honest, spontaneous reply. I thought our minds were running in the same channel. But yesterday! What are we to think of the right-about-face of yesterday, the straight contradiction of the spontaneously expressed views of last Thursday? Mr. Speaker, no wonder I have at times a feeling of frustration at such an exhibition. Which is Doctor Jekyll and which is Mr. Hyde? No wonder the country is perplexed. Nevertheless, let us go on. Let us do the best we can for king and country.
