speechtext: I did not interrupt the leader of the opposition (Mr. Hanson) during his address, although I must say that at times the relevancy of his remarks was rather slender as far as the subamendment is concerned. I just want to point out that there are rules to be observed in the house. I realize that in these war days perhaps the rules may be relaxed a little, but I ask hon. members to remember that my duty is to see that the rules are observed. Therefore, I wish hon. members would observe them more closely.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I shall endeavour to keep my remarks more closely to the subamendment than the leader of the opposition (Mr. Hanson) kept his, but may I suggest respectfully that all members of this house are entitled to precisely the same treatment. The treatment accorded to one member of the house ought to be accorded generally to all members who speak thereafter. I make this suggestion with all due deference to you, Mr. Speaker.
The subamendment reads:
And this house further regrets the failure of the government to adopt a monetary policy that would permit a maximum war effort without either increasing debt or reducing the standards of living below that necessary for maintaining maximum efficiency.
It expresses dissatisfaction with the present system and a desire for the reform of that system. We of the Cooperative Commonwealth Federation agree with those objectives, although we contend that the subamendment touches only the fringe of this great economic problem.
Last week the Minister of Finance (Mr. Ilsley) said that during this debate no member of the Cooperative Commonwealth Federation had expressed any disagreement in principle with the government's financial policy. However, we have done exactly that in previous debates. For example, on September 9, 1939, I said:
We should not inflict on the generation that follows us the cost of another great war. And we must not permit an increase in the already almost intolerable burden of national and other public debt. We believe that there are untouched financial resources which the government may still tap, or resources that have been only partly tapped as yet.
Again on June 28, 1940, I criticized the budget proposals and suggested certain alternative methods by which the government might raise revenue for our war effort. It is because we recognize the need for a more progressive approach to the problem of war production and war financing that we support the amendment calling for a reformed monetary system. We believe that our financial system ought to be considered as the accountancy system of our economic life. We feel that if we produce goods and services, the *money should be available to distribute and encourage their flow.
Miss Dorothy Thompson is a bitter but well-informed critic of the nazi and fascist regimes, and I have no hesitation in quoting her, nor do I expect to be misunderstood when I do so. She said:
The Germans did not vote themselves four billion money units for defence. They voted -had voted for them-thirty thousand planes, so and so many guns, so and so many thousand
The Address-Mr. Coldwell

tons of reserves of oil and raw materials. The German economy is an economy of things and men; the allied economy is an economy of symbols: money. The German economy recognizes that all wealth is in goods, particularly in capital goods, and that these are not created by money, which is only the medium of exchange, but by the application of labour to materials. The aJlies had money, but failed to produce goods. The Germans had no money, but did produce them.
I submit that by those words Miss Thompson clearly placed before the people of the allied countries a fundamental economic truth which the German regime has prostituted for a diabolical purpose, just as the devil can quote scripture when it serves his needs. Although we may dislike the prostitution of that fundamental economic truth, yet in these days when we are considering the expenditure of large sums of money we ought to pay some attention to methods other than those we have been using to finance our war effort.
The truth is that all material wealth results from the application of labour to material things. Once we realize that, the path to a better and brighter economic system will become more clear to us all. As long as we have men and materials we ought to be able to devise a monetary system which will facilitate the flow of goods and sendees into the channels into which we desire them to flow.
I have the New Zealand Hansard on my desk and I should like to turn to a speech made by the minister of finance of that country, Hon. Walter Nash, on June 27, 1940. As reported on page 307, he had this to say regarding the monetary and financial policies of that country:
Provision for loan contribution by large investors will be made by the issue of loans with a currency of ten years or more in respect of which government stock will be issued in the usual manner. In the circumstances the government consider that these loans should be regarded as contributions to the war effort from the material assets of those with property and should accordingly be free of interest for a period of three years or until twelve months after the conclusion of the war, and thereafter for ten years at a rate of interest not exceeding 2J per cent. In this way the government proposes to raise within New Zealand not only the money required to be expended in this country, but also some portion of the amount necessary to meet expenditure abroad, thus relieving, so far as is possible, the drain upon the resources of the British government.
Mr. Nash then outlined his proposals for a compulsory loan from those with large accumulations of wealth, and the necessary legislation was subsequently adopted by the New Zealand house of representatives.
Last week the Minister of Labour (Mr. McLarty) suggested a policy which will place a heavy burden upon labour. I submit, Mr. IMr. Coldwell.1
Speaker, that equality of sacrifice demands that a policy such as that outlined by the New Zealand minister of finance should be instituted here, and for the same reasons-to assist our own war effort and to help Great Britain in her economic and financial extremity.
Yesterday this was brought forcibly to our attention by the proposals that were made by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Ilsley) and which we shall have the opportunity of discussing later this week. But, holding the views which I have presented, I submit it is incorrect to say that we agree in principle with the government's financial policy. We are indeed in sharp disagreement with it. The Cooperative Commonwealth Federation in this house and throughout the country have stood for a different system.
Recently Mr. Herbert Morrison, Home Secretary in the British government, in the course of a speech in which he suggested- incidentally

definite war aims, as well as foreshadowed -a new monetary and economic system, made this significant statement:
If we are fighting only to end the nazi threat to our future, if we have no aim but to get back to pre-nazi Europe, we are chasing a will o' the wisp, and we shall fall into the mire. The roots of nazism are not all to be found in the original sin of the Prussian temperament: the roots of war lie deep in our present ways of living, and we have the chance now to dig some of them out. Upheavals and landslides there will be.
And, if I may interject this thought in
connection with the subamendment, one of these landslides will be against the present financial and economic system, sweeping it away and laboriously establishing order out of chaos, unless we at this time, when we have the opportunity, prepare now during the war to lay the foundations of a better and saner economic, financial and social order than we have known in the days that have gone by.
Mr. Morrison then went on to say this:
To-day, necessary measures to control our economic system in the interests of the community, and in the urgent cause of winning the war, are being resisted and attacked in the name of freedom. We need to be on our guard, evening -and morning, against this prostitution of a fine word. The freedom of private business is often another name for economic anarchy, which has always led to war-and always will.
May I point out that, while Mr. Morrison was speaking of economic aims, nevertheless, as a member of the British government he was not unwilling to place before the people of Great Britain some aims which can be interpreted as war and peace aims. He went on to say:
While we must be ready to surrender a measure of national sovereignty, we must maintain the cultural freedom of nations and a

The Address-Mr. Coldwell
proper measure of independence in their political life. We must cling to an ideal of government, whatever its actual form, as something which exists to serve peoples and not to dominate them.
Does our present financial system serve the people or does it to-day dominate the people? That is the question, it seems to me, which is involved in the subamendment.
And we must remember that this is no mere internal question, since the governments that dominate at home are often the peaeebreakers abroad.
Next, the nations must come together and tackle international economic problems, including the problem of colonial possessions, on international lines, even if this means the limitation of national sovereignty.
Then we must organize the industry, trade, commerce and raw materials of the world with the idea not of bolstering up the special privileges of any class or group, but of achieving a higher standard of life for all.
May I say that in my opinion that, too, is involved in the subject matter of the subamendment.
Next, we must insist upon achieving international control of arms manufacture and armed forces, once again giving up some of the old ideas of national sovereignty in order to bring that about.
Lastly-
He went on to say:
-the nations-victors, vanquished and neutrals alike-must agree that none will seek to be judge in its own cause. That each will submit its grievances and its quarrels to impartial judgment, and will abide by the outcome.
On that basis, Mr. Speaker, the British people have been rallied in support of a great cause. Some of us in the past looked with a good deal of apprehension to the war which was then coming, because in those days we had little faith in those who were associating themselves too closely with the dictator in Spain and with dictators elsewhere with whom they wished to make some kind of agreement. We should always keep in mind that our aims must include that every man shall secure the right to life, liberty and the pursuit of happiness; that he shall not be falsely imprisoned in gaols or in concentration camps; that he shall not be enslaved nor shall he be exploited to the profit of any of his fellows; and that he shall be free always and everywhere to think, to speak and to worship as he will. And may I say that these words are a summary of what Mr. Morrison went on to say. He is one of the men who to-day is inspiring confidence not only in the common people of Great Britain but in the common people of Canada and lovers of democracy all across the world.
I only wish that in our own country we could hear the same kind of challenging
economic, social and political aims put forward by our leaders at this time. If we heard them, I am convinced that there would be very little trouble about arousing the Canadian people to the necessity of bringing this war to a successful conclusion. But, on the contrary, those of us who hold these views in common with men like Herbert Morrison and Ernest Bevin, are derided and accused of giving allegiance to something our critics call state socialism.
We believe in more liberty not less liberty, in more personal property privately owned and enjoyed but not in public property privately owned and used for the exploitation of the Canadian people. To right the-wrong is the aim of the Cooperative Commonwealth Federation, and it is one of the-aims of the group sitting immediately to my left and embodied in the subamendment that, is before us this afternoon. The British workers are prepared to follow their leaders,, who have fought for their rights to organize and who have secured those rights for them in former days.
Although I usually dislike quoting at any length, I want to give one more quotation which I think has a direct bearing on the subject I am discussing. Mr. Henry L. Stimson, Secretary of War for the United States, in a speech at New Orleans on November 18, said:
Under the leadership of Ernest Bevin and Herbert Morrison, English workers to-day are producing as men have never produced before, and by their labour they are turning their island home into an unconquerable citadel of freedom. With the enemy's bombs literally dropping about them as they work, they are turning out more and more of the instruments of defence. This unconquerable effort has been made under the leadership of labour itself, which to-day is the backbone of the British fight for freedom.
Yet the political faith of Bevin and Morrison is under continuous fire in this house at the present time. In Canada factories are idle and men are unemployed because this nation is trying to wage war under the baneful influence of private enterprise with the profit motive at the root of its endeavours. This debate has revealed that there is not as much basis for the statement I heard from England the other evening from Air Marshal Joubert as I should like to think there might be. The Air Marshal was lauding Canada's war effort and saying that soon there would flow to Britain vast quantities of supplies from the war industries of this country. But this debate has shown that little or nothing is>
being done to prepare thousands of idle' workers for the day when our industrial life is organized, as it must be organized in the near future, for the task that lies ahead.
The Address-Mr. Caldwell

An estimate was made a few days ago that in addition to all the money that we require to raise, we shall require something over
200,000	new workers in industry in the course of the next few months. So far, however, we have scarcely done anything to train these workers for the work they will have to undertake. I do not agree with the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) that people who can milk can tend a machine. They require training to tend the complicated machines of our complex industrial life. The Minister of Labour quoted resolutions from labour organizations expressing their willingness to forego some of their basic rights. Let me say to the minister and to the government that if the working people of Canada are to be asked to forego some of their hard-won rights and privileges, then we must ask the owners of industry and the controllers of finance to share equally by the sacrifice of their privileges also. There is a growing feeling that this is not being done.
The defence of Canada regulations are being used to prevent labour from exercising the basic right to organize. We saw an example of that recently in connection with the difficulties at the Chrysler plant. Mr. Herbert Morrison declared that no man shall be falsely imprisoned in gaols or in concentration camps and that justice shall not be denied him or delayed. Yet in Canada there are many men who, although they may be guilty of having been members of subversive organizations at some time, nevertheless have the right, surely, to be tried-a right now long delayed-and to know what the charges are against them. Under the defence of Canada regulations justice, although not denied, is indeed delayed, because men are not getting an early opportunity to make their plea against the accusations which caused their detention. In this war for democratic institutions that right ought to be kept inviolable. Every man should have that right within the British commonwealth. We are not looking in the right places for the subversive influences. The arrest of humble members of society who make stupid remarks has been played up, and members of organizations now outlawed have been arrested only because they were associated with those organizations. Sometimes, not recently but several years ago.
This brings me to a matter which is allied both to the question of our own financial obligations and to the democracy for which we wish to use our financial institutions. It is a matter which in my opinion parliament must consider and consider carefully. In my speech at the beginning of the session I made some references to the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation and the resignation of Mr. Alan

Plaunt from the board of governors, and I requested that a parliamentary committee be set up to investigate the serious charges made by the retiring governor. I felt certain that the government would facilitate the establishment of such a committee in vieiw of Mr. Plaunt's long experience with publicly owned radio in Canada and the evident seriousness of the grounds for his resignation.
The Canadian Broadcasting Corporation is a public institution directly responsible to this parliament and not to the minister who may speak for it in this house. It is, therefore, a responsibility not of the ministry but of parliament itself. As I said in my earlier speech, radio is an important feature of modern life; through it, great good or evil can be done. I would emphasize that this is particularly true during a modern war and is a potent reason why we should maintain public confidence in this great and important publicly owned institution.
As yet no answer has been given regarding the appointment of a parliamentary committee. That being the situation, I think it is not unfair for me to assume that the government is prepared to allow the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation to continue its present policies and management without any immediate parliamentary investigation. As members of this house we have not only the right but the duty to inquire into the serious charges made by Mr. Plaunt. Are they well founded or are they not?
Last week the board of governors met and passed resolutions expressing confidence in the general manager. But it is significant that they did not say a word to meet the charges- and I use the word "charges" advisedly-that have been made publicly in the press and recited in the House of Commons. On the other hand Mr. Plaunt repeated his charges and emphasized them in a statement to the press after the board's resolutions were published. He says that, by failing to face the situation, the board was-I quote him-"condoning very serious internal conditions and irregularities as well as certain policies which are indefensibly partisan and harmful." Again may I say that Mr. Plaunt is a highy educated man, a graduate of both Canadian and British universities, and when he uses the word "irregularities" I submit that the use of that word is sufficient to warrant a parliamentary inquiry into the irregularity or irregularities alleged.
Moreover-and this is of the utmost importance-he reiterates his readiness to substantiate fully before a parliamentary committee the grounds for his resignation. In the face of these charges the board's expression of confidence in the management cannot be accepted

The Address-Mr. Coldwell
in place of a parliamentary inquiry. Mr. Plaunt's charges are in part directed against the corporation itself. Had the board been willing to take the necessary action, presumably Mr. Plaunt would not have resigned. In the public interest and in the interest of our democracy as well as of this great public service, it is therefore necessary to speak both plainly and bluntly in this matter.
Since the outbreak of war two important resignations have occurred from t'he staff of the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation, for reasons, so I am informed, which dovetail with the charges made by Mr. Plaunt. One of these resignations occurred shortly after the outbreak of war, and concerned a young Canadian who is well known to many hon. members. I refer, of course, to Mr. E. A. Pickering who had for some years been attached to the Prime Minister's office and had won a reputation for both his ability and, I presume, his loyalty. Mr. Pickering joined the corporation in the fall of 1938, and for the latter part of his one-year service held the position of assistant to the general manager. Yet, after less than one year's work with the latter gentleman, Mr. Pickering resigned, I am reliably informed because of unsatisfactory internal conditions and unsound practices. We have a right to know what those unsound practices were.

speechtext: My hon. friend has referred to Mr. Pickering's association with myself for a time in my office. From that it might be inferred by some that it was through this association in some way and with my knowledge that he obtained a position with the broadcasting corporation. I do not say that anyone is insinuating that, but I should like to make it perfectly clear to the house, and I am glad to have this opportunity to do so, that I was not aware of Mr. Pickering having secured any appointment with the broadcasting corporation until I read it in the papers. That was several weeks, or months, after he had resigned from his position in my office on the score of ill health. I just want to make that plain.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
I wish to thank the Prime Minister. I had no intention of making any such insinuation. The reason why 1 mentioned Mr. Pickering's association with the Prime Minister's office was that I thought it to be an indication both of his ability and of his integrity.
In view of the situation that has arisen in the corporation, Mr. Pickering should be invited to appear before a parliamentary committee and explain what unsatisfactory conditions and unsound practices caused him to tender his resignation.
Last week the resignation of Mr. G. W. Buchanan, son of a most respected western senator, was announced. Since before the outbreak of war Mr. Buchanan had been director of public affairs broadcasts, and had been employed in important posts with the corporation since the beginning of 1937. To the press Mr. Buchanan stated that his resignation was caused by "a lack of organization and clear definition of policies relating to war-time needs."
I understand that Mr. Buchanan's letter of resignation goes into the matter fully, and also cites a number of examples, which show a complete absence, in the present management, of any liberalism or sense of democratic objectives for which we are fighting in this war. In fact it would seem that, at times, personal considerations rather than the public interest have influenced the choice of programmes and speakers.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: Will the hon. gentleman permit me? Does he intimate in any way that there has been any malfeasance in office on the part of the management, or is it just a difference of policy? I would like him to elucidate that.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
I would say that the terms used, "irregularities" and "unsound practices" cover a much wider field than simply differences as to policy. Since those terms are used, I submit that it is the duty of this house to find out exactly what they mean, and that we should do so by way of a committee.
I was proceeding to say that some of the war programmes initiated by the corporation itself since the outbreak of war have done this country no good. Hon. members will recall, for example, the broadcasts by Mr. George McCullagh and the circumstances attending them. They will also remember, perhaps, a series called "Over the Top," which I am reliably informed was stopped through the intervention of the government itself.
We have had some excellent war series, but upon inquiry I have learned, or at least have been told, that all of them originated in the office of public information, or in one of our own government institutions or departments. A parliamentary committee could place the responsibility where it belongs.
I come now to a matter of equally grave importance. In the November 23 issue of Le Jour, a newspaper published in Montreal in the French language, which I read with some difficulty, there was a long article, which I had translated for me afterwards, signed by the editor and dealing in part with the behaviour of the Montreal management of French network of the broadcasting corporation

The Address-Mr. Coldwell
towards Jules Romains, one of the greatest living figures in French literature. I propose to place the following extracts from the article-a translation of course-on Hansard:
The Canadian Broadcasting Corporation, too, thought it prudent to forbid any political speech by the author (Romains) over its network. He was told that he would be welcome at CBF-
That is the French language broadcasting station.

if he would confine himself to a literary subject. Naturally the offer was declined. Romains had broadcast more than once from American stations. These broadcasts had been relayed to Canada. They were, perhaps, the finest and most useful talks, from the viewpoint of our war aims, that we had heard in Canada. Why then did Romains, once here, become for these scrupulous CBC officials, a scapegoat and a pariah? We know-and we will prove it at the proper time and place- that there are, in the higher reaches of the information and radio services, men who not only have always been and still are the enemies of the democratic ideals for which thousands of our men are shedding their blood, but who, while hypocritically praising-because it is the duty of their office-the acts of our allies would in no way be displeased by a British defeat and a nazi-fascist victory.
I am quoting, of course.
We know the company these people keep, and in those circles it is quite the correct thing to do to vilify England and to judge with philosophical calm-and even with sympathy- Germany and Italy. And yet, these are the men who are paid to mold public opinion, to steer hatred into the proper channels, to create enthusiasm, in brief, to save us! We are indeed in good hands! It is by having acted in this way, it is by having harboured in their midst saboteurs and traitors, that certain European countries, including France, are to-day humiliated and enslaved.
I deeply regret to have to unveil this shameful situation. I do it because it is my duty and I hope that the government at Ottawa, before whom I place these facts, will be wise enough to open its eyes and to act.
These are most serious charges. Mr. Jean-Charles Harvey, the author of this article, states that he is prepared, at the proper time and place, to prove these charges. There is only one proper place, Mr. Speaker, and only one proper time. That place is before this parliament, or a committee of this parliament, and the time surely is at the earliest opportunity. Therefore I submit that the statements by Mr. Plaunt, the grave charges made by Le Jour, and the reasons given for the resignations of Mr. Pickering and Mr. Buchanan surely demand a complete investigation into this important public service, which we must protect, as a public service, from destruction before it is too late.
Why is the government silent on the matter? No reference was made to the corporation in the speech of the Minister of 
Munitions and Supply (Mr. Howe) in this house. Why does the board of governors remain ready to allow such a condition to continue? This is a great public service, and to my mind it is dangerous to rely almost wholly upon a chairman who is the head of a St. James street trust and a vice-chairman who is a key figure in the Canadian movie industry, which in a sense is a competing industry and which, largely under the guidance of this same vice-chairman, has become one of our great Canadian monopolies. Is this another example of big business controlling what has been called by a United States author the " opinion industries?" I repeat that conditions in the broadcasting corporation, our experience since the outbreak of war and the incidents to which I have referred demand a complete parliamentary inquiry into the whole matter, and I am taking this opportunity of again asking for such an inquiry, or an assurance by the Prime Minister that it will be undertaken when the house reconvenes in February.
There are other matters to which I should have liked to refer, but I see that Mr. Speaker is warning me that my time has expired, and I do not wish to trespass further on the time of the house.
Mr. JEAN-FRANCOIS POULIOT (Temis-couata):	Mr. Speaker, I am sure hon.
members must remember quite well what happened last August, when the leader of the opposition (Mr. Hanson) suggested that we should not prorogue but that, instead, the house should sit for an indefinite period of time. I believe the views of a majority of hon. members were not those expressed by the leader of the opposition, who leads-I wonder whether that is the proper word- just a small handful of members of parliament. His idea was that the house should be adjourned to some later date, in order that we might be able to meet in case of an emergency. Strangely enough, the date on which we met again was November 5, not the date of the invasion of England by Hitler but the date of the presidential election in the United States, an altogether different matter. The house met and parliament was prorogued; two days later this session was begun and this debate has continued since that time.
I wish to offer my most sincere congratulations to those members of parliament, whose number is growing every day, who have shown their independence of thought in offering constructive criticism. For many years I have done that, in language that was not always flowery but nevertheless was always sincere. At times, sir, I have been treated like a

The Address-Mr. Pouliot
black sheep because I spoke my mind, but I felt vindicated when I heard or read the fine speeches made by some of my colleagues this session. Members of parliament realize their responsibilities, which are heavy, and I am glad to say that our constituents realize them also. I am amazed that a small number of cabinet ministers should think this is their own war and their own business, and that they can lord it over us. It is time they realized that it is our war, the war of all of us; our business, the business of all of us; our money, the money of all of us; and our future, the future of all of us.
In saying that, I am not at all advocating a union government, nor is it my idea that the leader of the opposition alone should be taken into the confidence of the government. I believe that when matters of importance are to be decided by the government, all members should be taken into their confidence. We are here as representatives of the people, with whom we keep in touch. Every week-end since the beginning of this session I have returned home to meet and talk with my constituents, and I am prouder of them than ever. I feel refreshed when I go home; in fact, if I had not spent my week-ends at Riviere du Loup I could not have stayed in Ottawa for so long this session.
But, sir, at times each of us has. occasion to meet a man on the street. We talk to him and, what is more important, we listen to him. I say that because no member of parliament will learn the views of his people if he proceeds to give a lecture. He must ask questions. He must listen, and must remember what has been said to him. When the poorest man in a constituency pays any member of parliament the honour of calling on him, and when that person opens his heart to show confidence in his representative, and tell him secrets he would not tell his neighbour, that member may well be proud of his position as a member of parliament.
When we assemble in this chamber we have the duty not to forget what we are told by those who have honoured us by permitting us to represent them. I want to remember what I have been told by them. There is not a member in this house who does not wish and expect-and the sooner the better- the complete defeat of Hitler and Mussolini, and all of those who would try to impose their will on the democratic nations, and cause them to disappear as such.
There are few of us who are in the army. It is our duty to see that a real war is waged against those whom, by passing two orders in council last year, this government has declared our enemies. They are the enemies
of all of us, and we must win over them. The winning of this war is essential to the welfare and to the future of all democracies.
I am reminded of what Marshal Foch said in my presence at the Chateau Frontenac in Quebec, when he was received after the last war as the victor over the hordes he had defeated. His words were: "War is common sense." As we shall all be affected either favourably or unfavourably by the results of this war, it is our duty to give all possible assistance to the government, and to tell them we are one in our desire to help to win.
But I wonder whether flattery is a real help. I do not think it is. When one is driving a car along a dangerous highway and he sees his friend raise his hand, and hears him say, "Do not go farther," that person must not conclude that his friend has become unfriendly simply because of his action in giving warning of a danger. The natural thing to do is to stop and to take heed of the advice given. One may ask, "Why have I been stopped?" And the answer might be, "There is a precipice at the end of this road, and if you proceed two hundred yards farther you may fall over it."
With this in mind, I say that there is nothing hostile in the action of a member of parliament who warns the government against any dangerous policy. One of the worst policies we could follow would be that of thinking that we are to come here simply to listen to everything that is said, and observe "de Conrart le silence prudent"-"Conrart's prudent silence." At times we have something of praise to say; at other times we may have blame to place. But so long as a man is sincere, no person must expect him to become a slave, or to be ready to swallow everything decided by persons outside the government who have no right to speak on behalf of the people of Canada.
We are facing a long, hard war. Everybody is agreed on that. We shall not win it by shutting our mouths and being yes-men. Members of parliament should be consulted, and sooner or later the government would have to make up its mind about it. Matters of great importance and vital to all of us are decided by a handful of anonymous outsiders who believe that they are high above criticism. The man who enters politics or public life, even from the back-door, has no right, whenever it suits him, to retire under the shelter of his private life so as to escape criticism. To give the reason that it is ungentlemanly to criticize the actions of the experts whose advice is blindly followed by the government is ridiculous. As members of parliament we are all exposed to such
The Address-Mr. Pouliot

attacks. When they are unfair we are at liberty to justify ourselves. If one is afraid of them, then there is only one thing for him to do, and that is to stay at home.
In these days we hear a good deal about Westminster. Let us follow what is being done at Westminster. We should act as they do there, so far as parliamentary practice and procedure are concerned. The rules of that house are not numerous, but the practice has been established by traditions stretching back hundreds of years-traditions of freedom, traditions of liberty, traditions of real democracy-and the parliament at Westminster should be our guiding star in our deliberations. Otherwise we might forget that we are a British dominion. Anyone who might visit the English parliament would see that men have an opportunity to discuss questions vital not only to Great Britain but to the whole of the British empire. They do so freely. They are not afraid to speak, nor do they use the language of sissies. They talk like men, and man to man. The atmosphere of Westminster is not that of a pink-tea room but that of the oldest parliament in the world, one in which the members show that they are men, that they are worthy of the confidence placed in them.
I can tell you, sir, that I am true to the traditions of my province, true to the traditions of my family and true to the traditions of the illustrious grandfather of my chief when I make these statements. I have always been ready to defend my party. I have always believed that one should be loyal to his party, and I have tried to show fidelity to mine at all times. I have shown fidelity when the whole party was ready to vote for Bennett. I was alone in voting against him. I have shown fidelity to the party when everyone on our side had a long face after hearing two speeches by the Hon. H. H. Stevens about unemployment. I ask hon. members to refer to what he did and said about it during the time when Mr. Bennett was leader of the opposition, when he was Prime Minister and after the great good-bye. He disappeared and we did not see him round the house any more for a whole week.
The same with the former leader of the opposition. I can remember when he sat with dear old Ned Ryckman during the time our party was in power in 1928. Between the taking of two votes Mr. Manion tried to make a surprise attack on this government, and I answered him. My first word was that this was the first time in my life that I had noticed the effervescence of a cerebral seid-litz. Some hon. members were laughing, but I was defending my own party. That happened before dinner, and after dinner the

whip came to me with a five o'clock edition of one of our Ottawa contemporaries and showed me the report of a speech which had been delivered by Sir Robert Borden the same day. He told me to use it because the first part of that speech was directed against the prospective Tory leader in the house.
There were times when we were fighting for the party, fighting against R. B. Bennett, the man who was defying God and man, and was just as scarlet as that thing under the beak of a turkey. I told our lamented friend, Mr. Rogers, to give me a chance to fix him. I told him a few things which were quite right, judging by the way in which they were received by members of the party. Then he sat down. It was said that that was a wicked way to deal with the former Prime Minister. And he was still red.
Every time the party has been in trouble the member for Temiscouata has defended it because he expected at all times that the party would promote views which would be in the interests of the people of the country. This was done for a long time. This was done until 1930, the golden age of the Liberal party. You, Mr. Speaker, were a member of the house at that time, and you will recall the great days until Bennett came to power. Then what happened? Bennett had the opportunity to show how good he was as Prime Minister of Canada, but look at the type of men he picked for high positions in the government service! He picked pygmies from the United States and from all round the country. When Mr. Bennett was Prime Minister, they never knew what was going to happen the day after; but when this government came into power, it was decided that they were experts, that they were gifted with the faculty of being mind-readers and so on. It is deplorable to think that such importance is given to men who are not in contact with the Canadian people. There are many of these men in the service, particularly in the Department of Finance.
I have listened to my hon. friends to my extreme right and I appreciate the fine optimism they show in the subamendment. But that optimism is preceded by pessimism. The subamendment reads:
And this house further regrets the failure of the government to adopt a monetary policy-
Here comes the optimism.
-that would permit a maximum war effort without either increasing debt or reducing the standards of living below; that necessary for maintaining maximum efficiency.
It has never been clear in my mind just what they wish to promote. When I have asked them they have answered that I did not understand a word of what they were

The Address-Mr. Pouliot
saying. Of course, I am simply a man on the street, I am not an expert in these great problems of finance. Then they asked something with which I cannot agree absolutely:
Furthermore this house is of the opinion that a continuation of the present financial policy will further destroy the precious liberties so essential to, and recognized as being inherent in a true democracy.
I cannot say that I agree entirely with that. There is, however, something which we can discuss together and with regard to which we can arrive at a certain understanding. In my opinion the worst possible policy to adopt in connection with financial matters in this country is that of contraction. If a man attempted to live on a diet of vinegar and lemons, he would be finished in no time, because those articles of food would have the effect of contracting his stomach so that it would be impossible for him to eat anything else. One of the absurdities regarding trade which were advanced by R. B. Bennett was that trade should be one-sided, that we should have no imports but should just export to other countries. He did not consider invisible exports in connection with the tourist traffic and so on. This was a great mistake, and I am afraid that the experts of the Department of Finance may induce this government to follow that practice. Most of these men were Bennett appointees and therefore they are dangerous men. They were advisers of Bennett, and I think this government should take their advice with at least a grain of salt.
For five years we had as Minister of Finance a man who had absolutely no legal training or understanding. He never knew the rules of the House of Commons, and he was inclined to follow the same dangerous course as had been followed by Mr. Bennett, and listen to men who were not qualified to occupy the high positions they hold in the Bank of Canada and the Department of Finance. They were his advisers-men who were cranks. I remember very well that one day I was interrupted by the then Minister of Finance, who took the advice of a man who was then and is still incompetent, in the Department of Finance, and he is one of a great many lords of this country whose advice is followed by the government. He has one of the highest salaries paid in the civil service. Another one, who receives $30,000 a year, says to all the poor fellows who have no money, "Tighten your belts; practise economy." And he receives $30,000, enough to sustain sixty families during this hard winter. Those are the people we are expected to listen to. They are the experts, they are the great men, they are the Melehizedeks. Well, that is enough.
We are told that it is not gentlemanly for us to say that these men are not qualified to be considered experts in this country. I strongly protest, Mr. Speaker. They should be fired, all of them, and replaced by men having sound minds and good common sense.
We find the same conditions in other departments. Men come from outside and are deemed to be experts. So long as they have not been elected by the people they are great men. One of the ministers, who I presume is now the guest of the Right Hon. R. B. Bennett at Juniper Hill, Surrey, told us that we were not to indulge in favoritism or in patronage. Let us look at the directors and officials of Barclay's bank, the bank of which he was a director, who are now in the Department of National Defence. There is Magee, there is Fraser, and how many more. When these -things are done by the department, it is all right, but when a request is supported by members-"nix.". What hypocrisy it is to tell us that there will be no politics in -these matters, and yet all these barons of finance are coming here to take possession of Ottawa! We shall never stand for it. I am all against this kind of thing. If these men want to have anything to do with public business, they should run as candidates in a constituency, or be appointed to some vacancies in the senate, or be made deputy ministers.
To-day we have a czar of labour. We have also a czar of steel. Besides that, orders in council during the recess are substituted for the statutes of parliament, because the government has followed the absurd proposal of the leader of the opposition. It is not the usual statute book which we are supposed to receive, it is orders in council passed during the adjournment which are the laws of the land, and I would not be astonished if such orders in council are still being passed while this parliament is in session and while we have been discussing and listening to commencement exercises.
Well, sir, I hope we shall soon come back to the good old system of responsible government. We hear at times from ministers that they have assumed a great responsibility- that they have decided this or not done that, and by so doing have assumed a great responsibility. Of course it is the duty of members of the government while in office to make certain definite decisions regarding the matters which are brought before them; they have to decide what to do. But they do not assume thereby any extraordinary responsibility; they are there to discharge those functions, and whether they do the right -thing or not is a matter for the House of Commons to decide.
The Address-Mr. Pouliot

Ministerial responsibility is the rendering of accounts for every cent which is spent by the government. That is ministerial responsibility, it is understood by all of us, and it was well expounded by the hon. member lor Rosthern (Mr. Tucker), who made one of the most magnificent speeches that I have ever heard in this house. Ministerial responsibility is a principle which our forefathers fought for, and they succeeded in gaining it, and now we have lost it since Charley Dunning has been Minister of Finance. Hon. members recall the discussion of the mortgage bank, when he told me that he had given me information. He had, indeed, given me some information, but it was not all that I wanted, and I did not get any information about some of the bodies for which the Canadian taxpayer is responsible.
My idea of responsible government is so important, Mr. Speaker, that, as it is one minute to six, I will ask you to call it six o'clock. I have something else to say.
At six o'clock the house took recess.
After Recess
The house resumed at eight o'clock.

May I refer again to the subamendment? The first part reads:
And this house further regrets the failure of the government to adopt a monetary policy that would permit a maximum war effort without either increasing debt or reducing the standards of living below that necessary for maintaining maximum efficiency.
We have of course to consider the question of inflation, because we cannot forget what happened to rubles, marks and francs in consequence of inflation. But even with inflation it is impossible to improve the standards of living without increasing debt, and we have the example of the United States of America, where marvels have been accomplished for the unemployed, but not without increasing debt; and, as every hon. member knows, the debt of the United States is the largest of any country in the world.

speechtext: Why can it not be done without debt?

speechtext:
Therefore the subamendment is contrary to common sense. If put into practice, it would not work. In my humble view it is necessary to have a currency standard. When our mint was under the British government we had reports on coinage, but unfortunately, since the mint has become Canadian, we have not.
When all the gold reserve of the world is accumulated, concentrated and frozen in one

country, the currencies of other countries are depreciated to that extent. What standard shall we have in the future? A possible standard is silver-and I cannot see how we could have any other precious metals than gold and silver as standards of currency. Platinum is, of course, a very rare metal, and no one could expect the standard to consist of diamonds or other precious stones. At any rate, a standard is needed. Whether in the future it will be silver we do not know, but we do know that if neither gold nor silver is accepted as the standard, then we shall have to go in for barter, and that is the primitive method of trading.
We must rely on trade and on trade moving both ways, and I congratulate the government warmly upon having sent a trade commission to south America. I wish every success to the minister who is going there. It is a step in the right direction. The monetary system should be looked at from the point of view that money is not the principal factor, being only the medium by means of which trade is carried on; and if anyone makes it the principal factor, he is making a great mistake. For these reasons it is impossible for me to vote for the subamendment.
May I say one word to my hon. friends to the extreme right. If they cite the Aberhart administration in Alberta as a success in the field of social credit they are quite mistaken, because the management of Alberta's business affairs by Mr. Aberhart has been more conservative than if it could have been in the hands of Sir Herbert Holt.
There is another point I wish to make and it is this. If the first part of the subamendment were deleted, I would vote for the second part, for this reason. In the Bank of Canada and in the Department of Finance we need, not economists but bankers-sound bankers-and I take this opportunity to offer my congratulations to the Minister of Finance (Mr. Ilsley), who honours me by listening to what I am going to say about him. I am going to pay him no mean compliment. May I say that he has intelligence-a thing we have not seen for five years in the heads of that department. In the second place, I believe he is sound-minded and I put him in the class of the late Jim Robb, whose budgets were always so well received by the country. The Minister of Finance can take my word for it that it is no mean compliment I pay him when I compare him with the late Mr. Robb, because Mr. Robb was a man of common sense. Indeed, he was a great man precisely because he had a great deal of common sense. He was no fool.
A great mistake has been made in finance in Canada. As I once pointed out to that

The Address-Mr. Pouliot
great financier who had become rich overnight-I refer to R. B. Bennett-the national debt is in a large measure the national wealth; and if a country pays returns upon an amount borrowed from Canadian citizens, these returns are the income of our fellow citizens. Therefore it is dangerous to reduce the rate of interest on either dominion or provincial loans; for, if the total amount of interest which is to be paid by the dominion and by the provinces is less, it means that the returns to those who have lent money to the Canadian exchequer, or to the exchequers of the provinces, as the case may be, will also be less, so that a certain amount of disturbance results. Of course, it is the policy that has been followed for some years, and in my opinion it was a great mistake.
Interest on bank deposits has been reduced, and interest on the shares-the return to the shareholders of the banks-is about the same. That also is a mistake. Take a person who has $20,000 in a bank. When the rate of interest was three per cent the return was $600; now the rate of interest is only one and a half per cent and the return is only $300. The result is that, owing to that reduction in the rate of interest on deposits, that person has to begin living on the capital itself, and little by little the deposit disappears from the account.

How about the widow who

Well, I understood only
the word "widow." You see, sir, it is elementary that one should look at both sides of the matter, but only one side is seen, the side of the government. Of course the country pays that, the provinces pay that, but the people of our country are poorer every time.
There is another thing I cannot understand. It is that the issuance of bank notes in Canada is guaranteed by the national reserve in gold and other securities. Of course the reserve must be in the hands of the institution that issues the bank notes; that is
elementary. But with our experts-and this is a point I was going to make last session when I was answering one of my hon. friends on the extreme left and was interrupted by my hon. friend the Minister of Mines and Resources (Mr. Crerar) who is just coming in and whom I welcome; he did not seem to understand the point-on the one hand, the bank notes are issued by the Bank of Canada, and on the other, our national reserve in gold and securities is in the hands of an altogether different institution, the foreign exchange control board. How can the foreign exchange control board guarantee the payment of bank notes, "pay to the bearer," issued by the Bank of Canada? I cannot understand it, it must be very high finance.
At one time, according to the statute books of this country, it was necessary for a man to have ten years' experience as a banker to be deputy minister of finance. But now it is superfluous.
Banking is a science, and political economy is not. Banking is a science based on rules of experience; political economy is only a conglomeration of views concocted together. One may have one view, another may have another view, a third may have a different view, a fourth a different one again, but it does not mean that from all these views you will make a science. A science is definite, real knowledge. That is what I want for those who are in charge of this delicate problem of finance for this country.
If there were only the last paragraph of the subamendment, I would vote for it because I find that Canada is in a very dangerous situation by reason of the ill-advice that is given by some so-called experts both in the Bank of Canada and in the Department of Finance. And it is impossible to get any information about that. Last year I tried to get the telephone numbers of the Bank of Canada, and my hon. friend the Minister of Finance told me "No. 369;" that was repeated nine times. But it was No. 369, meaning that there were at least 369 telephones in that square building.
I have much more to say, but I will do so on another occasion.

Mr. Speaker, I have already spoken on the main motion, and therefore will not have an opportunity to speak again in the course of the present debate if I do not take advantage of the present moment to do so. Possibly I shall not be violating the rules of the house if, in speaking on the amendment to the amendment, I confine my remarks to replying, in a very few particulars, to one or
630	COMMONS
The Address-Mr. Mackenzie King
two things that were said this afternoon by my hon. friend the leader of the opposition (Mr. Hanson). What I might wish to say with regard to what has been said by others can perhaps stand over for another time. But I believe my hon. friend would expect me to reply to him immediately, or at least in the course of the present debate.
Perhaps my hon. friend would let me begin my remarks at the place at which he concluded his. His last remarks had reference to the statement which I made in the house yesterday and which, much to my surprise, he characterized as quite unexpected and something much more critical. May I first of all say to my hon. friend that the reason why I made the statement I did yesterday, rather than wait until a later day in the session, was that on Thursday last when he asked me to give the house information with respect to existing conditions, he said that I ought to give the information either that day, or at the latest, "to-morrow", which was the word he used, "to-morrow" being Friday. I replied that I would wish to think over what I had to say before speaking on a matter so important and might wish a little longer interval of time. I was anxious to reply to my hon. friend just as soon as I could after he had made the request he did, not only to oblige him in that particular but also because I thought the statement which he made was one which called for a reply at the earliest possible moment.
The statement which my hon. friend made left in my mind, and I think in the minds of all hon. members, the impression that a condition existed in Europe at the present time, a condition which, as he expressed it himself, was very much worse than it had been at any time since the fall of France. We all know that at the time of the fall of France the condition was as bad as it could possibly be. Nothing could have been more serious than the situation was at that particular time.
My hon. friend asked me to make statements of a specific character. He is right about one sentence of what his request contained; it was:
I would request him to indicate what further, if anything, Canada can do at this juncture towards aid and assistance, whether it be in men, materials, supplies or equipment.
I felt that the statements which had been made by myself and my colleagues in the course of the present debate had answered that question in very large part before it was asked, inasmuch as they set forth a programme which the government is doing its utmost to carry out, and which I think all will agree is as extensive as could be expected at this particular time. But I did conclude

by saying that I thought the situation demanded all that all of us could do. I wish to say at once that I think the time has come when people everywhere throughout Canada should realize that they must examine their own consciences, as well as seek to look into the conscience of the government, to understand what service they can and ought to render at a time as critical as the present. Each man or each woman in Canada knows what he or she in his or her present circumstances can do to assist Canada's war effort. Some can assist by saving, others by lending; some can assist by working in one direction, others by working in another direction. The time has come now when it is for every man or woman to ask himself or herself, "How can I where I am, and where I may find it possible to 'be, best serve in this great crisis; how can I serve my country and how can I serve humanity itself?" because it is the existence of civilization as we understand it that is at stake at this time.
The government is putting forth all the effort it possibly can, as a trustee of the people. The government's task is to take account of the fact that it is dealing with the funds of the people of Canada. It is not dealing with matters that are the personal property of its individual members. The government is a trustee, having to discharge duties on behalf of the people of Canada as a whole; and in discharging those duties it has to have continually in mind its obligation of trusteeship with respect to what can be done at this stage, what may havq to be done to-morrow, and what may have to be done at a still later time.
Here is the specific statement my hon. friend wished me to make. These are his words:
... in my view, in the view of many hon. members of this house, and I feel quite certain in the view of many people in Canada, the war situation in Europe is more serious to-day than at any time since the fall of France. The virtual destruction of the cities of Birmingham, Bristol and Southampton, the loss of shipping as evidenced by press reports, and in particular the utterances of the Marquess of Lothian, his majesty's representative in the United^ States, particularly with respect to finance, indicate the seriousness of the position.
Then my hon. friend goes on to say:
Therefore in my view the Prime Minister should make a statement to the house and the country, if not to-day then not later than to-morrow, and tell the country just what the exact position is; because it will be understood that he has access to information wrhich we have not. Let him tell the house and the country how serious the position is or, if we are wrong in our views, how good the position is. . . .
I ask hon. members who listened to the statement I made yesterday if I did not in

The Address-Mr. Mackenzie King
every respect try to follow literally the request of my hon. friend. I tried to tell the house how good I thought the situation was. I also tried to tell the house how serious I thought the position was. I do not think I overemphasized the one or the other. I did direct particular attention to the inference that could be drawn from my hon. friend's words, because later on he repeated them, when he said:
.. . I do feel that the situation to-day in the theatre of war over there is just as serious as it was at the time of the fall of France, and we are all very uneasy about it.
I do not feel that way, and I could not reply to my hon. friend that I agreed with him in that. To-day my hon. friend says that in my reply I agreed with him that the situation was serious, and that he could not understand why I went further in the statement I made yesterday. Here is what I said in reply to my hon. friend, quoting the words that he would wish quoted:
I agree with my hon. friend in his view that the situation is a serious one. I think anyone reading the press would gather that opinion. I would also say that such information as the government itself is receiving the press would appear to be reflecting accurately. Any statement that I may have to make will be practically in accord with what has already appeared in the press.
What did my hon. friend say when I concluded my statement yesterday? He said I had not told the house anything the house did not know or anything that had not already appeared in the press. I fail therefore to see in what I said where there was anything that should have called forth the remark my hon. friend made in referring to the statement I had given. The hon. gentleman said that, recalling what I said on Thursday last, he felt a sort of sense of frustration as I was speaking yesterday; that he wondered which was Doctor Jekyll and which was Mr. Hyde. I would say to my hon. friend that I have been wondering what could have brought to his mind that work of fiction by Robert Louis Stevenson on the strange case of Doctor Jekyll and Mr. Hyde; and I have come to the conclusion, since my hon. friend spoke about what Mr. Brockington had said as a result of his close association with me, that he must have had in mind some of the correspondence that had passed between Mr. Brockington and himself, before making the remarks he did in the house this afternoon. I do not know whether my hon. friend regards the correspondence that passed between Mr. Brockington and himself as confidential. I do not think he does, because he referred to it this afternoon and, indeed, quoted a passage from it.

First of all, he asked for a copy of the speech that was made at Philadelphia, and then he said:
I assume, of course, that you were speaking in your own personal capacity, but if you went there either representing the government or in any manner interpreting the government to the American Bar Association it would be a matter of great interest to me, because I understand that you made the following declaration on that occasion . . .
In speaking to the house this afternoon, my hon. friend approached the subject from the point of view of Mr. Brockington's close association with myself, and sought to have the house believe that what Mr. Brockington said at Philadelphia was as a result of that close association, that he had been saying something there which differed from what I had given to my hon. friend as a statement of the facts of the case. Mr. Brockington immediately sent a copy of his speech to the leader of the opposition, and my hon. friend thanked him for it and said:
As a piece of sheer oratory, it is magnificent.
I salute you, and congratulate you.
Elsewhere he went on to say:
But I do wish you would write me and tell me frankly what you had in mind when you spoke, near the end of your speech, of "a pact ' between your country and mine by which you

agree to defend us in certain eventualities and we agree to defend you," and what you know, for I was assured on August 20 by the Prime Minister that up to that time there were no commitments and I have not heard of any since.

speechtext:
I do not
exempt myself from doing that at times. We are all prone to do it. But I do say to my hon. friend that holding the positions he and I hold at this very critical time, we owe it to ourselves and to the country to be most

careful about the words we use in stating matters which relate to this all-important situation.
My hon. friend was referring to Canada's war effort, and to an impression concerning it which, he says, exists in Great Britain. I must say I was very much surprised at the remark of my hon. friend. I thought I had his exact words before me, but I believe I can recall them almost exactly. They were to the effect that from information he had received from the other side of the water there was a feeling in England that Canada is seeking to make money out of our war effort. I ask my hon. friend just to think about the significance of those words. That is not an attack on the government; it is an attack on the people of Canada. That is a reflection upon the war effort of Canada as it is being put forth by the producers, by manufacturers and by all the men and women in this country who are seeking to do their part toward the winning of the war.
My hon. friend tells us that, despite all we have been seeking to do-and I use the term "we" in the sense of the people of Canada- that in England there exists the impression that Canada is seeking to make money out of her war effort. I say that is unfair to the people of England. I say it is unfair-yes, doubly unfair to the people of Canada. I would go farther and say that it is a libel upon Canada that anyone should either express or repeat words to that effect-anyone who has any understanding or knowledge whatsoever of the war effort of this country.
I think I am as much in touch with leading persons in the old country as is my hon. friend the leader of the opposition. Not a day goes by that I do not receive some communication from the old country in the form of letters or telegrams in reference to the views entertained there with respect to Canada's war effort. Hardly a day passes that I do not meet someone, or converse with someone who has just come from the old country or who has been there and just returned home; and I say to my hon. friend that the word they most use with respect to Canada's war effort is that it is magnificent [DOT]-that is the word. And I say to my hon. friend that if anyone expressed to him views such as he indicated this afternoon, he did not know what he was talking about.
My hon. friend has said that we should do all we can to dissipate that view. May I say to him that I have not heard another citizen in Canada express a view of the kind. It is my hon. friend who has put forth that view, and he is the only one who has done so.

The Address-Mr. Mackenzie King
I want the people of Canada to know that no one in England has any opinion of that kind with respect to Canada's war effort.
I come now to the other side of my hon. friend, the better side. A few days ago my hon. friend spoke of the desirability of the house appointing two standing committees. I believe he made that suggestion on November 12, when he first spoke in this debate. His words were as follows:
Knowing of this feeling I am impelled to propose to the government that it cause to be set up immediately two select special committees which will be charged with the responsibility and the duty of investigating and reporting to this house factualy, objectively and truthfully, without bias and without partisanship-and I have no doubt that is possible- what is our exact position (a) with respect to our fighting forces, military, naval and air; and (b) with respect to the production and delivery of all the important materials, equipment and supplies necessary in our war effort, so that the Canadian people may know the truth. Before such committees ministers could appear and be subject to questioning.
My hon. friend concluded by saying:
I am willing with some of my colleagues to meet with the Prime Minister and some of his colleagues so that we may consider the whole proposal, in an honest effort to arrive at a conclusion.
May I say that since making that statement, my hon. friend and two of his colleagues have met with me and two or three of my colleagues to consider the matter there referred to. I wish to say to him and to the house that no approach to the subject could have been more helpful or could have been better in every respect than that which he and his colleagues made in confidence with the government in this matter. We spoke quite frankly to my hon. friend and his colleagues with respect to the difficulties which surrounded the procedure of dealing with war expenditures, questions of production and distribution- deliveries, I believe, was the word he used- in any standing committee of the house which might be holding its proceedings in public and which during part of the time might have to ask that the proceedings be held for some time in camera. We particularly pointed out the difficulties of imparting to parliament or to any committees certain information.
I will mention to the house just what one of those difficulties is. We have been asked by the British government-and this is a request they have made to governments in all parts of the British commonwealth; it is not one which has been made to us alone; it is a matter of which the British government itself has taken full account-to avoid, if possible, the disclosure of numbers, the disclosure of amounts, the disclosure of quantities, the
disclosure of anything in public which would help to give the enemy an appreciation of the strength or lack of strength of the forces opposing him.
I think every one can see the reasonableness of a position of the kind. But it does raise a very difficult situation for the government. If we are not on the horns of a dilemma, we are at least in the matter of information sailing between Scylla and Charybdis all the time. We are either too near the rock of Scylla in giving more in the way of information than we should, or we are drifting to the other side toward the whirlpool of Charybdis and are being accused of withholding from the people of our country the information they are entitled to have. I can only put the situation as it is in its clear light before members of this house and before the country, and trust to the soundness of their judgment. That is the position we are in with respect to the disclosure of information that might prove to be harmful.
As I have said over and over again, it must be remembered in connection with this present conflict that it is not a matter of days, it is not a matter of months, but it is a matter of years. Information that we are giving from hour to hour and from day to day is being accumulated by those whose interest it is to do all they possibly can to destroy the British empire and every part of it. I believe our country is fairly free of those who have played the disreputable part which has been taken by fifth columns in other countries, but that we are wholly free of persons who are gathering up information to pass on to the enemy, sorting it out for them and telling them the significance of it, I do not for a moment believe. Therefore, we have to be scrupulously careful of what we say, having regard to human nature as we know it, and having regard to the situations as we know they have been in every land.
It is for that reason and for that reason only that the government hesitates to say to this house that it is prepared to have standing committees before which will be placed the exact position with respect to our fighting forces, naval, military and air. Let me illustrate: With respect to our air force, it would mean that we would have to tell how many planes we have been manufacturing, how many have been sent across the seas, how many airmen are being trained, when they are likely to leave Canada, how many have sons, et cetera, et cetera. I have, I am sure, only to mention this to have hon. members see its significance. Then, with
634	COMMONS
The Address-Mr. Mackenzie King
respect to the production and delivery of important materials, equipment and supplies necessary to our war effort, I have only to point out that to state in public what we have shipped and are shipping in the way of supplies, where they have gone or are going, is simply to give to the enemy the kind of information he is most anxious above all else to have.
I agree with what my hon. friend has said about the position of private members in this house. Every member is anxious to become more actively interested in Canada's war effort. I think one thing my hon. friend said this afternoon is very much to be emphasized. There is no greater part that hon. members can take in Canada's war effort than it is possible for them to play in their own constituencies where they are known and trusted. They can tell the people of their constituencies all that they possibly can with respect to the war effort and what they know is needed in order to make the war effort successful. But that is not enough. Hon. members are right in feeling that they would wish, that the house itself would wish to make its own contribution to the war effort in some way. The government, I can assure hon. members, is most anxious to have it do so in any way that is not going to make for confusion but will help to carry forward this tremendous task. I can assure hon. members that we desire their fullest cooperation.
This afternoon my hon. friend made a suggestion which appeals very strongly to me for more reasons than one; first of all, because of the proposal itself, and also because it is the procedure which on this very perplexing matter has been adopted at Westminster. In the parliament at Westminster the government has been faced with exactly the same situation we are faced with here. They have of course a much larger number of private members than we have in this House of Commons and their private members are as anxious to make their contribution as are our private members. They are on the firing line, and one can imagine the intensity of feeling there must be with respect to the desire on the part of every man to do what he can during the hours he is in parliament as well as when he is at home in his constituency.
The British government are making expenditures on a much vaster scale than we are, and human nature is the same in the United Kingdom as it is in Canada with regard to all classes and conditions of men and how they may act in respect of government contracts and large quantities of money and supplies at a time of war. They are just as anxious as we are to see that whatever is done is done

openly, honestly and above-board and to bring to time summarily anyone who seeks to profit by opportunities which war conditions may afford. But they have not thought it advisable to set up standing committees of the character which was originally proposed by the leader of the opposition. They have however, established a committee on national expenditure which has been given certain powers and which has been functioning now for almost a year, having been set up on December 12, 1939. On November 7, 1939, Sir Archibald Sinclair, who was then leading the Liberal party in the House of Commons, asked the Chancellor of the Exchequer whether he could make any statement on the appointment of a committee on national expenditure on the lines suggested in a motion to which my hon. friend referred this afternoon.

This motion reads:
That a select committee be set up, similar to that appointed by parliament in July, 1917, to examine the current expenditure defrayed out of monies provided by parliament for the defence services, including civil defence, and to report what, if any, economies, consistent with the execution of the policy decided by the government, may be effected therein.
Sir John Simon in his reply outlined briefly the measures already being taken to ensure economy, but added that he appreciated the desire of the house to make its own contribution to this end. He said:
The government consider that this object would be best attained by setting up a select committee on national expenditure with terms of reference which would broadly follow those under which the select committee was set up during the last war. The select committee would deal with expenditure connected with the war whether civil or military.
He said that the committee would be set up at an early date, and the committee was set up on December 12, upon a motion being passed. Before I quote the motion, may I say that after careful consideration of the whole matter the government is prepared to introduce a similar motion into this house and to follow the procedure which has been adopted by Westminster with respect to war expenditure. As the leader of the opposition has rightly said, the committee on public accounts is not adequate at the present time to deal with the vast expenditures that have to be considered. The committee on public accounts has referred to it the report of the auditor general which contains expenditures of the previous year. My hon. friend, the

The Address-Division
leader of the opposition, wants a committee which will have the power to review current expenditures.
May I say, speaking for myself and I believe for all my colleagues, that anything that is going to assist the government in seeing that the right control is exercised over the expenditure of monies in connection with this war will be more than welcomed by the administration. I want to add that whoever is appointed to such a committee ought to take his responsibilities very seriously. Great care will have to be taken in the selection of the personnel. If there is a genuine desire to do the thing that is helpful, I am sure that great good can come out of the existence of a committee of the kind. If, on the other hand, the committee is to be made an instrument for party warfare, I cannot conceive of anything that could be worse.
