But I repeat that if a committee of the kind were to be used as an instrument of party political warfare, I cannot conceive of a way of working greater injury to Canada's war effort. But a committee which takes its responsibilities seriously, and will assist the government in exercising a control over the expenditures which are being made, keeping on the government the responsibility for policy, but being free to make suggestions that will be helpful and constructive, should be of the greatest possible service. It was that kind of committee which on December 12 last was set up at Westminster, and this is the motion under which action was taken:
That a select committee be appointed to examine the current expenditure defrayed out of moneys provided by parliament for the defence services, for civil defence, and for other services directly connected with the war, and to report what, if any, economies consistent with the execution of the policy decided by the government may be effected therein.
I propose, Mr. Speaker, as soon as parliament reassembles after the adjournment, to introduce a motion in those words in this House of Commons. I say, after the adjournment, because I think hon. members will agree that we can much better begin establishing a select committee of this house at
the moment of continuing its regular proceedings, rather than at the beginning of the Christmas recess or within a month of meeting shortly thereafter. I hope this assurance will meet with general acceptance.
In taking my seat, may I again thank my hon. friend and those who were with him for the manner in which they discussed this whole question with my colleagues and myself, and also for the constructive suggestion which he has made in this particular.

speechtext:
I have just a few words to say about this amendment. I express my great surprise about the way in which it is drafted. The hon. leader of the opposition (Mr. Hanson) follows the practice of his former leader and flees away when I start to speak. I remember the time when "R. B." was leader of the Tory party; as soon as I rose he went out, and the same practice is followed by his illustrious successor.
But, sir, I will take the amendment as it is; I find it an insult to the intelligence of the Canadian people, and especially the farmers. Here is that masterpiece of Toryism-I put on my glasses and I will read between

the lines. They all run away, they are all afraid, they are hares, they run from the battle, they are all from Taranto. Here is the amendment:
. . . that this house regrets that the government has continued to soothe the Canadian people regarding the war effort of the nation, thereby creating a false sense of security when a clear-cut call to action is desperately needed.
What does that mean? Nobody knows. It reminds me of the time when Mr. Bennett's Minister of Labour was introducing some legislation, and when I asked him the meaning of that legislation he was unable to answer; he did not know. When I asked the leader of the opposition to-day for the meaning of the words "realistic attitude" that he used in his speech, he was just as dumb as Wesley Gordon was when I was asking questions of him in the glorious time when Mr. Bennett was in supreme command.
The Canadian people want information, but information that can be useful, useful to us as members of parliament for the good of the soldiers, sailors and airmen of this country. A distinction should be made, and it shall be made, between a check on the total expenditure on the war and information about the movements of the troops and so on. The hon. gentleman did not make any such distinction.
I do approve, however, of one of the suggestions of the opposition, that of having a secret sitting at which members of parliament could be fully informed with regard to all phases of our war effort.
Part of the information they insist on getting is information that should be given, but in camera, not in public.
I am surprised that of the great men in the front line of the Tory party none has added very much distinction to the discussions that have taken place in this chamber. What are the words of the amendment?
We respectfully submit to Your Excellency that this house regrets that the government has continued to soothe the Canadian people . . .
I could read what the dictionary says about the word "soothe." It mentions "to soothe a wound," but this government did not wound the Canadian people. The wound was inflicted by the Bennett regime, of which the leader of the opposition was a member for a few years. This government has had to patch up that wound. I wonder whether I should have used the word "soothe" when the leader of the opposition was turning his back to you, Mr. Speaker, and making some sounds across the floor of the house. No one knows what is meant by that word, and I fear that something is wrong; I fear there was

The Address-Mr. Pouliot
some malicious intent on the part of someone in not explaining it to the leader of the opposition. Then the amendment continues:
.	.	. thereby creating a false sense of
security. . . .
I ask you, Mr. Speaker, how this government creates a false sense of security. Again nobody knows what that means; the leader of the opposition and all the marvellous speakers of the Tory party who have bored this chamber for so long have not explained that. Then it goes on:
. . . when a clear-cut call to action is desperately needed.
Was it a clear-cut call to action when, at Charlottetown, the leader of the opposition betrayed information that the British government had asked to be kept secret? My right hon, chief was amazed that the hon. gentleman should disclose such information.
Then there is the hon. member for Davenport (Mr. MacNicol), who is gifted with the eloquence of an auctioneer, who wanted to launch a convention to replace the present leader of the opposition. It is not a year since the hon. gentleman was chosen, and already they wish to replace him. Whom could they get? The leader of the opposition tried another idea in Quebec; he sent all the defeated Tory candidates a questionnaire asking what they thought of him. I could tell him what was said about him by the two official organs of the Liberal party in the province of Quebec, Le Canada of Montreal and Le Soleil of Quebec. I conceived it to be my duty to include those quotations in a letter which was published in the best weekly issued in Canada, Le Saint Laurent of Riviere du Loup. This is what Le Canada of September 12 had to say about the hon. gentleman, who was one of the nonentities of the Bennett government:
Mr. Hanson is against everything, even common sense.
I might translate that roughly as " Mr. Hanson is against everything, even common sense." Later the Minister of National Defence for Air (Mr. Power) stated that Hitler was the latest recruit to the Tory ranks; a fine compliment. Through the medium of the local newspaper I said to my electors:
In advising the prime minister not to adopt the Conservative leader's suggestions, your representative sought to avoid for his leader the embarrassment of accepting counsel from a tory "who is against everything, even common sense" (according to Le Canada) and "who has Hitler as a recruit" (according to the Minister for Air).
Then the great Quebec Liberal organ, Le Soleil, had this to say:
The tory leader shows his true calibre.
Mr. Hanson's importance derives principally from the position he is occupying temporarily at the House of Commons, that of acting leader of the opposition. In this capacity, notwithstanding his harum-scarum nature, he is treated with respect by the Prime Minister, the Right Hon. Mackenzie King, who informs him, on occasion, of facts and projects of a confidential nature. Mr. Hanson has just taken undue advantage of this privilege, in the hope of putting himself in the limelight and of striking a treacherous blow at the government.
(Editorial of Oct. 12.)
We have not sufficient space to reproduce here all the editorials Le Canada has since devoted to the leader of the Conservative opposition. Here are the choicest titles: Oct. 14-"Mr. Hanson at the head of his class: first in the Fifth." This editorial purports to state that if Mr. Hanson had spoken thus in England he would now find himself behind the barbed wire of a concentration camp, as leader of the fifth column. On October 16, Le Canada calls him a "circus clown" and on October 18, the same newspaper wonders: "What is delaying Mr. Hanson's resignation?" This edition also contains, on the same page, a second editorial on the subject. It is entitled: "De Profundis", and concludes with: "Here lies Mr. Hanson."
The translation of the last sentence is "Here lies Mr. Hanson." I attach no great importance to that, but the newspapers of my province have recited the de projundis on him; let him now rest in peace. But there is something to this amendment; the second paragraph reads:
And this house further regrets that despite the serious condition of agriculture no effective action is proposed to alleviate that condition and to ensure to the Canadian farmer a just, fair and reasonable return for his products.
I do not wish to do what I blame others for doing, Mr. Speaker; I do not want to turn my back to the chair. We must remember the time when R. B. Bennett was Prime Minister, the time of the iron hand. We discussed butter in this house; butter, which had been the subject matter of lengthy discussions on the hustings throughout the country; butter, that golden treasure which was melting away and returning no benefit to the farmer. The house met; the then Minister of Agriculture was the late Mr. Weir. The Bennett government introduced some , legislation. They put a high tariff on butter; and the higher the tariff went, the lower fell the price of butter. My hon. friends behind me remember those days. We were asking questions of the then Minister of Agriculture. I was asking R. B. Bennett who had imported such vast quantities of
The Address-Mr. Pouliot

butter from New Zealand and Australia, because I had information, which I knew to be accurate, that this was being done by the Tory party.
I am glad to welcome my hon. friend the leader of the opposition back to his seat. He must remember also that when I asked his then leader, the leader of the Tory party, who had imported such vast quantities of butter, causing prices to fall lower and lower, he would not answer. It was a secret; apparently it was impossible to learn who had done that. But everyone knew that the Tory party had put some money in the market for speculation, and that the lower the prices of commodities went, the higher became the profit for the Tory electoral fund. Butter was purchased by the Tory party in Australia and in New Zealand, so that the price of our own butter fell. Hon. members opposite, who were then sitting in the house, will recall that when I asked questions of the then Minister of Agriculture he was unable to answer them-and neither was R. B. Bennett himself, or Wesley Gordon, or Sir George Perley, or Mr. Sauve, the then Postmaster General, or Mr. Duranleau, or the present leader of the opposition when he was Minister of Trade and Commerce.
These are the gentlemen who say that farm products are not selling well enough to-day. What is their record? Can we ever forget it? In those days farmers received the rock-bottom price for butter. That drop in price began in the first year of the Bennett regime, due to the high tariffs which were then advocated for the relief of the farmer. They did not dare speak about it afterward.
Then there was an imperial conference of some kind before which Mr. Bennett spoke about the possibilities and potentialities of hogs and bacon. Well, he never had success such as the present Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) has had, in selling to Great Britain large quantities of bacon, for which the farmers will receive reasonable prices. We want to have some real help for the farmers. We find it strange-to use a mild expression-to hear hon. members opposite refer again to the plague which may affect the farmers, especially in view of the fact that conditions were so bad under their management. "A just, fair and reasonable return for his product"-that was the language used by all Tory spokesmen on the hustings during the campaign of 1930.
I see in the house many of my hon. friends who defeated Bennett ministers. For instance, I see the hon. member for Kamloops (Mr. 
O'Neill) who conducted a wonderful campaign, and did particularly well in his constituency. He was victor in the cause of Liberalism. And there were so many others I cannot name them all. They did well because the people-farmers and labour-were fed up with the policies of the Bennett regime.
Someone may tell me that this kind of talk is untimely, that it is uncalled for in a time of war. But my point is that those who were incompetent in time of peace cannot be geniuses in time of war, just because we are at war. Those who have been no good in ordinary times cannot be excellent in extraordinary times.
I am reminded of what was said to me about the Tory leader in the senate on an occasion when he was being praised most lavishly. The person speaking to me was relating that the Tory leader in the senate had been born under a special star, and that his gifts were as numerous as the stars of the sky and the sands of the sea. I was surprised, and asked for more detailed information on the point. I said, "By the way, what have 'been the great accomplishments of that illustrious gentleman? Can you name in his whole political career a single accomplishment which has served the Canadian people, one piece of legislation which has been useful to the country?" "Well," he said, "he has been very unlucky." That was the description of the leader of the Tory party in the senate by one of his best friends.
Why should we pay any attention to the demands which come from the other side? The people in this country say that the Liberal party has a mandate to govern in war time, and we ought not to pay any attention to demands by the leader of the opposition or any of his satellites. The government should carry on the war effort boldly and honestly and get rid of all those Tories who are a perpetual nuisance and who are committing sabotage in the departments in which they hold important positions. Get rid of the Tories-that should be our watchword. Get rid of all the Tories who infest some of the war departments, and then we will receive no blame from them. Why do they blame the government? They do so because it is too tolerant with them. The government does not deprive them of their positions. Well, let us put them all out; let us put all the Tories out. Let us get rid of them, in order that we may have a sane administration in all departments of government in Canada.
Of course they are greedy for more power. The leader of the opposition knows what I mean. I could name some Tories who have

The Address-Division
insulted my leader and members of the government, but who are now deciding from whom goods for soldiers shall be bought. Everybody knows that. When there is a leak in the Department of National Defence, it comes from a Tory who is there-and I could name him. They are there, and they are impudent. Not only that, but when Tories are in power, Liberals can get nothing; no Liberal can be appointed. But when the Liberals are in power, we hear the Tory members saying, "Oh, let us have no politics; there should be no patronage." And they raise their hands, as if they were praying, and one would be led to believe that they are praying all the time.
We know that the people of Canada have judged them; they had enough of their rule. My only suggestion is that the government should keep away from bad company. I ask the government to pay no attention whatever to any suggestion from the leader of the opposition respecting four months of training or anything else. I presume his suggestions are made in good faith, but they are inspired by those in the department who desire more power so that they may betray the ministers they should serve faithfully. That is all.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, like our beloved sovereigns who, every day, disregarding great dangers, convey their most compassionate consolations to the unfortunate victims of the London bombardments, Her Royal Highness, Princess Alice, wife of our most distinguished Governor General, has also shown commiseration for the suffering which has so cruelly stricken the population of the Magdalen islands, which bear the heavy brunt of these war consequences. Her merciful appeal to the population of Canada in her speech to the Women's club on October 7 last has warmly cheered and deeply moved the hearts of these unfortunate people. In their name I have the honour to extend to her royal highness the tribute of their most respectful and sincere gratitude.
Such examples of great heroic magnitude and Christian charity, as given by Buckingham Palace and Rideau Hall, are an infallible token of survival in the most crucial tests. They strengthen the ties of a people to the present regime and the liberties they enjoy under it by convincing them more firmly that, between two contending forces the British might, based on the immutable principles of love and justice, will assuredly triumph over the other force, sustained as it is by hate and by the tyrannical yoke of a despotic Gestapo.
Mr. Speaker, if I felt I should address this house in English, the language spoken by the majority of hon. members-and in spite of difficulties my pleasure in doing so is very great-it is as a tribute to my Englishspeaking electors of Gaspe and the Magdalen islands, whose great patriotism in the present war I wish to praise.
The various ministers of the crown have eloquently submitted to us accounts of our war effort. May I submit to this house another account, that of the contribution to that same war effort of the most ancient section of the country, the county of Gaspe and the Magdalen islands, which I take great pride in representing here.
The patriotism of our population has not weakened since 1914, when it has given more than one complete regiment. The long and glorious list of its sons who died on the field of honour, and whose names one can read on the pedestal of the monument erected at Gaspe in their memory, is sufficiently eloquent
[Mr. Pouliot.J
to render unnecessary adding anything to its testimonial.
At the outbreak of the war, in September, 1939, men of all ages and coming from all walks of life volunteered their services in numbers so large that they could not all be accepted at once. Of over 1,300 volunteers serving in the army, and a few in the navy, there are many French-Canadians, but the majority belong to the Loyalist stock and to the other English-speaking Gaspesians. The population of only 8,000 of Gaspe and the surrounding district has alone supplied some 600 volunteers. At Grosse-Ile and Entry island to the Magdalen islands, all the young men and many married men have volunteered their services and are serving in the army or in the navy. If we count those from the other islands, they are in all about 200 in number.
In proportion, these enlistments from Gaspe and the Magdalen islands must hold the record for the whole of Canada. Had all parts of the dominion furnished volunteers in the ratio supplied from Gaspe, Canada to-day would have for overseas service an army of over 320,000 men. And above this contribution in men, our population, according to its means, has heavily subscribed to the war loan and has contributed to welfare societies such as the Red Cross.
This readiness of the Gaspesian people in helping the country during critical hours can be explained by the peculiarities of their character in constant contact with dangers which are their daily companion and allurement.
One anecdote, out of thousands, will convince and help hon. members in reaching a deeper understanding of this class of labourers whose valour and merits are generally too much ignored. I will relate a drama of the sea which happened at Riviere-au-Renard, on September 28, 1936.
On that day the fishing was good and fishers had kept the sea until they were compelled by a tempest to come back to the shore, but one boat continued to battle the high seas. It was the two brothers, Phileas and Peter Tapp, reputed for their courage and ability, who were still fishing.
At three o'clock they decided to make for the shore. Three miles from the shore their overladen boat was capsized by a huge breaker and the fearless fishermen were plunged into the sea.
On the shore their comrades and other people witnessed in consternation this horrible drama. The infuriated sea, lashed by a strong wind, which is customary on the coast in

The Address-Mr. Roy
the fall, seemed a challenge to the bravery of these men to come to the rescue of their brothers.
However, the sad victory of the sea was not to be complete. On the crest of a wave we could see the two castaways clinging, one to the stern and the other to the sternpost of the capsized boat, with the grip of their last hope. Four young and sturdy fishermen, Jules, Maurice, Isaac Dufresne and Ephrem Couillard, fortified by their courage, succeeded in launching another boat a few miles below and in reaching the scene. After three hours of struggle this boat was wrecked as it reached the shore. But Phileas Tapp was saved, although, unfortunately, his poor brother was lost.
Even on the battlefields could feats of such heroism and positive bravery be accomplished? The whole history of Gaspe and the Magdalen islands is made up of these and still more pathetic episodes. Every autumn we have to deplore these disasters and often would-be rescuers perish in trying to help imperilled fishermen.
Unfortunately, this admirable population, so full of virtue and of the most generous patriotism, is ill-paid for its devotion and sacrifice. The Magdalen islands settlement is battling against the pangs of the worst misery. Precarious as their situation was last Bummer, it has now become desperate. May I tell the house what this situation is and what has caused it.
The lobster catch was good enough, but the sale at the minimum price fixed by the government resulted in a deficit. The codfish catch was sold at a better price, but the sale was very small and that of mackerel was a lamentable failure. A few thousand barrels were sold at a loss and the rest, some
20.000	barrels, is a complete loss. About
60.000	boxes of smoked herring are on dealers' hands, if not sold at a loss.
This is the balance sheet of the expired season which has left the fishermen in debt and without any means to secure such essentials as flour and fuel to survive during seven long winter months, when there is no possibility whatever on the islands of earning a single cent. The old saying, "the end of fishing is the end of eating," is now an acute actuality.
To these distressing prospects is added another one. In a few days, navigation with the islands will be closed and it will be practically impossible to come to the rescue of this population before spring.
The Red Cross made a survey in the beginning of November in order to give assistance, but it is not likely that this society will be in a position to give enough assistance
in fuel and flour to meet the needs. It must be remembered that there is no fuel whatever in the islands. Meanwhile, what are the governments, federal and provincial, doing to relieve this distress? Have they answered the numerous calls for help from local authorities, the press and, yes, from Her Royal Highness Princess Alice? Have not these people, who are a component part of confederation, paid their taxes and given soldiers for the defence of the country and of democracy?
Moreover, is it not true that the state is helping other classes of producers whose product is undersold? The law of the land permits the granting of direct relief to destitutes and the spending of moneys for relief works. Why is it that these two remedies have not been applied since the government has not deemed it proper -to accept the advice of those who advocated a minimum price on fish, as on wheat, or the purchase of the surplus as has been done for apples?
There are two reasons which explain the indifference and lack of sympathy of the two governments for these destitute fishermen. The first is probably the fact that these fishermen are not sufficiently known, nor are their merits appreciated. The second is, perhaps, that the county is represented in the Ottawa and Quebec parliaments by an opposition member. In the first -case the anecdote I related a few moments ago should help in reviving a more fraternal sympathy for these people. In the second case, may I say that the time is ill-chosen to exercise sanctions of a partisan nature against a population which accepts so generously its great share of the war sacrifice.
A population so well bred, and answering with such readiness the call of duty, should not be ignored and chastized for its political opinions or abandoned to its fate when abnormal circumstances drive -it into destitution. Let the government take urgent and necessary measures to relieve most distressing cases, and let it also strive to remove the causes of all these evils.
Coming to the speech from the throne, may I now discuss the most essential aspect of our war effort. One of the striking notes of the government's policy, in recent days, is the increasingly insistent appeal to national unity, and the tribute to the loyalty of the province of Quebec. It is well and fair to extol our loyalty; but care should be taken not to give the impression that our loyalty has been revived or is of recent date. No; our loyalty is not of yesterday, nor is it any deeper than it was in the past.
The mention of such illustrious dates as 1787, 1812 and 1849 is sufficient to recall the fact that the retention of Canada under the British allegiance is due to the loyalty of the



The Address-Mr. Roy
French-Canadians to the British crown. I need not point out the value of this service rendered then by my race. I may say, however, it has made confederation possible, and justified the fathers of confederation in saying that there are no victors and no conquered race in Canada.
As a vivid example of our loyalty and patriotism, one can mention the admirable attitude taken in the present war by the greatest and most distinguished French-Cana-dian of our times, His Eminence Cardinal Villeneuve.
Three reasons explain the greatness and persistence of our patriotism. First, it has been tested and has suffered. Second, French-Canadians, having remained royalists, are loyal to the British crown by reason of the fact that politically everything separated them from France of the revolution. Lastly, we cherish Canada more than others because we cherished Canada long before others did and with a more exclusive Canadianism. Our Canadianism which cautious and wise men have always upheld in the past has nothing of the dangerous excesses of that campaign inspired by partisan motive waged in Quebec in the last twenty-five years. After such a campaign the wise and rational stand taken by Quebec in the present war is highly surprising. We must realize that French-Canadians have not been led to revolt by demagogues as they were at the time of the former national registration in 1917.
Let the government of the day, and more especially the Minister of Justice (Mr. Lapointe) and the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Cardin), take this into account in recalling the past to which they were no strangers. This political past explains why the government feels the need of appealing for national unity and loyalty, and the remarks I now make are in support of the following amendment which I propose to submit:
We respectfully submit to Your Excellency that by reason of striking contradictions between your advisers on principles which should guide our war policy and war effort this house regrets that your advisers do not give sufficient guarantees to ensure national unity.
We also respectfully submit to Your Excellency that by reason of the fact that Your Excellency's advisers from the province of Quebec in this house have asked a mandate in pledging themselves to participate in the war in a moderate, free and voluntary manner, this house is of the opinion that these advisers have no mandate to carry this war effort to the ultimate limit.
Mr. Speaker, has national unity always existed? Is it yet existing in the midst of the cabinet and the ministerial ranks? Has the Liberal party always worked for its

realization? Was it in the interests of national unity to propose during the last war, on January 17, 1918, the breaking of confederation as it was proposed in the Quebec legislature by the Hon. J. N. Francoeur who, with the support of the Minister of Justice (Mr. Lapointe), was elected federal member for Lotbiniere in 1937? Was it in the interests of national unity to charge the Prime Minister of Canada (Mr. Arthur Meighen) with being the executioner of the French-Canadians, as was done in 1921 by the then mayor of Montreal, Mr. Mederic Martin, who is now a Liberal member of the Quebec legislative council; or to allow the most influential Liberal paper of Quebec, Le Soleil, to say on October 24, 1925, that Mr. King's policy is "not one cent will be spent, not one man will be mobilized for the empire"?
Was it in the interests of national unity to raise the Turkish war scare in 1926, and the Egyptian war scare in the 1930 elections, and to allow to be printed on July 25, 1930, in La Presse a false London cable entitled, "Conscription Menace", with a warning from Senator Raoul Dandurand, the Liberal leader in the Senate, a warning which has not yet been denied? Was it in the interests of national unity in the last Quebec provincial elections to raise the cry, "A vote for Duplessis is a vote for conscription"?
Therefore it is not surprising that those whose political fortune has been made by these appeals to prejudice feel the need to protect the national unity for which in the past they had very little consideration.
Since the government is asking for unity in mind and motive, is it not fair to ask whether this unity is in the mind and motives of the government? Is there unity in the Liberal mind when Hon. Mr. Pattullo, Liberal premier of British Columbia, stated on August 9, 1939, that if Great Britain were at war Canada would help her to the last man and to the last dollar; and, when the same Hon. J. N. Francoeur, who had proposed during the last war the breaking of confederation, stated at St. Fabien on December 19, 1937, " I am emphatically opposed to the spending of one cent to equip and send one man to foreign wars?" No sooner had this statement been made than the Minister of Justice said, " Mr. Francceur's cause is mine; his victory will be mine." And on the polling day, December 28, the Prime Minister telegraphed Mr. Francoeur, " The electors of Lotbiniere have voted as Canadians who place national interest above all."
What can be said about unity in mind of the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner), who on February 6 last stated at Markinch that the Liberal party was opposed to con-

The Address-Mr. Roy
scription of wealth and conscription of men even for the defence of Canada? This is a Canadian Press report which has never been denied.
Did the Minister of Justice not state in Quebec on December 13, 1938: "Instead of going to war abroad we will stay here?" And did his colleague, the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Ralston), not affirm on February 28 last: " Our first line of defence is on the English channel?"
Again, what can be said on unity in mind of these other two ministers, the Minister of National Defence for Air (Mr. Power) who, at St. Fabien on December 13, 1937, said: " I went to the war, I came back and will not go again and will not send anyone to the next war," and the Minister of National Defence, who stated in Montreal in September last: " Canada in this war is at the side of Great Britain and the Canadian first line is in England?"
Can we find any unity in mind between the Minister of Public Works and his leader? None whatever. The Minister of Public Works declared in Montreal on January 14, 1938, that in the event of Great Britain being at war with Italy he would say to Canadians, "Stay at home;" and he added "This is my government's policy."
The government's appeal for national unity would be more convincing were the Prime Minister trying to reconcile the Minister of National Defence for Naval Services (Mr. Macdonald) with the Minister of Public Works. Speaking in New York on October 24 last, the Minister of National Defence for Naval Services said: "We have sent men and ships and guns and planes over the seas, and we shall send more and still more, so long as there is a single Canadian dollar left to be spent or a solitary Canadian citizen to take his stand in defence of freedom." Only three days later, the Minister of Public Works, speaking at St. Ours, stated: "We will never approve compulsory enlistment for overseas service."
It appears that unity in mind is also lacking between the Prime Minister and his colleague the Premier of Quebec, Hon. Mr. Godbout, who, at Plessisville on November 17 last, stated: " The mobilization act is the most anti-imperialist law put in force by the Canadian government."
To lead his party out of this other valley, the valley of contradictions, the Prime Minister should try to reconcile his own statements on the main object of this present war effort. In fact, in this house on November 12 last he stated:
. . . it was not this party, it was not the members on this side of the house that created
a "Canada first" policy and tried to educate the Canadian people in their attitude towards interimperial relations on a "Canada first" point of view. At the time the "Canada first" cry was raised I protested against it as strongly as I could.
That is to be found on page 40 of Hansard for this session.
But, speaking on foreign policy in this house on March 30, 1939, the Prime Minister stated:
We are and will remain Canadians, devoted, first and last, to the interests of Canada. . . .
In view of such conflicting declarations it is not surprising that in Montreal on
January 15, 1938, Hon. Fernand Rinfret should have said:
When, in the past, there was participation it was in spite of us, Liberals! We, Liberals, we are for Canada, for Canada after and Canada only.
When has the Prime Minister protested as strongly as he could against this cry of his own colleague? After having been spurred by so many contradictory statements and pledges by the Liberal party, we readily realize the urgency of appealing for national unity. Circumstances seem to have favoured Canada in keeping this party in office at the last elections, because that is the most effective way to keep it under censure. In peace time the Liberal party has constantly opposed participation in foreign wars, and I can hardly understand how it can now change its policy to one of participation to the extreme limit. The Minister of Public Works tried to explain that when speaking at St. Ours on October 28 last. This is what he said:
The government policy has not changed and will* not change.
It must be one thing or the other. The government has fooled the province of Quebec if its war policy then was its policy of to-day, or it is fooling the rest of Canada now if its present policy is still its antiimperialist policy preached in the past. The truth is that in every electoral campaign since 1917 the Libera] party has promised throughout Canada, with particular insistence in the province of Quebec, that Canada will not any more participate in any empire wars. After having declared war on Germany in 1939, it altered its former attitude in the last Quebec provincial and federal election campaigns by promising that there would be moderate participation only. To-day according to the Minister of National Defence for Naval Services, the limit will be reached only when there is not a single Canadian dollar left to be spent or a solitary Canadian citizen to participate. What an evolution!
The Address-Mr. Roy

It has been said and repeated many times that the Liberal party is a party of expediency. Its greatest electoral successes have been achieved in times of distress by the exploitation of the miseries and sacrifices of the population and of its good faith. This shameless opportunism should not guide the policy of the government in war time, but it seems that the government is pursuing two efforts, the first that of winning the war and the second that of maintaining the huge electoral machine of this oligarchy which controls everything.
There should be only one effort based on the dollars and sacrifices of the poor and the rich; that is the effort for victory. The other should be immediately sacrificed to the first; loyalty and patriotism require it. Since in the name of Canada we are asked to sacrifice our liberty, our wealth and our lives in the service of democracy, have we not the right to ask the government to abandon its partisan ambitions? It is necessary that we ensure national unity, and that must be realized at once and at any cost. To do this it is essential that a policy be clearly and frankly defined which will reconcile the conflicting opinions which it would be dangerous to allow to exist any longer in the cabinet and in the nation. What good would be all the sacrifices generously made in our country to ensure the triumph of democracy over oligarchy in Europe if, after the war, we had to admit that democracy had been killed in Canada by the poison of the oligarchy which is being imposed upon us?
In support of the amendment I wish to quote an editorial from the New York Times of October 9, following Mr. Churchill's famous speech:
It is one of Mr. Churchill's supreme gifts to democracy that he has put furtiveness and concealment aside in dealing with his countrymen.
Nothing is so anti-democratic as furtiveness and concealment between the government and the nation. Duplicity and furtiveness are the Liberal past. Duplicity and concealment are its present. For these reasons I have the honour, as a National-Conservative-Independent member, to move the amendment I read during the course of my speech.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as you are
well aware, I had not the slightest intention of taking part in this debate. Although the amendment of the hon. member for Gaspe (Mr. Roy) has not found a seconder, I believe it my duty to say at least a few words. I shall be brief.
With the first part of the hon. member's address I am almost completely in agreement. We sympathize with the distress of the fishermen of the county of Gaspe, and in helping them we certainly will be happy to second the efforts of the various associations and even those of my hon. friend.
In one particular, however, I must take objection to what he says. He stated that the government did not come to the help of the people of Gaspe because they are represented in this house by a member of the opposition. My hon. friend is, to some extent, boasting. As he well knows he does not represent the majority of the people of the county of Gaspe, so his argument fails to the ground. The huge majority of the electors of Gaspe are behind this government. The hon. member was elected by an unfortunate accident. There were two strong Liberal candidates in the field who had divided the Liberal vote. I predicted on the night of the election that, because of that division, the constituency of Gaspe would be the only one which would send an opposition member to the House of Commons. That happened.
My hon. friend is welcome in the house; but he must know he is here because of a division in the Liberal ranks. So the hon. member has no right ho say that we are not listening to the claims of Gaspe for political reasons, because Gaspe is Liberal, and will prove to be Liberal at the next election. I ask my hon. friend in all sincerity and in all earnestness if he thinks that his speech has contributed anything toward helping Canada in this tremendous conflict. Has he helped in any way?
Here we have a gentleman who has just voted in favour of an amendment which I shall read-and his electors will know all about that. That amendment states in part:
We respectfully submit to Your Excellency that this house regrets that the government has continued to soothe the Canadian people regarding the war effort of the nation, thereby creating a false sense of security when a clear-cut call to action is desperately needed.
My 'hon. friend has voted for that amendment. He thinks that the government is doing

The Address-Mr. Lapointe (Quebec East)
nothing in its war effort, and that we are lulling the Canadian people into a false sense of security. He believes that we are not giving a clear-cut call for action, as my hon. friend would like to have it. Yet this is the speech he makes in the House of Commons and this is his clear-cut call to action.
My hon. friend's speech-and he must have seen it himself, because he is intelligent-has created a painful impression everywhere in the house, even among his friends who sit round him.

The hon. member suggests that my colleague the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Cardin), my other colleagues from Quebec and I are creating disunity in our province. When I make that statement I do not speak politically; I speak rather of parliament as a whole, and indicating that my hon. friend is alone in his view.
Quebec is solidly behind the effort of Canada in this conflict, and we are going to stay solidly behind that effort-no matter what may be the sniping campaign of those disgruntled politicians who try to divide a united country. The hon. member for Gaspe has had the audacity-and I ask pardon for using the word-

"Audacity" is not contrary to parliamentary rules; the leader of the opposition (Mr. Hanson) uses words much stronger than that. I say that the hon. member for Gaspe has had the audacity to say that during the last provincial campaign there was a cry in Quebec that a vote for Duplessis was a vote for conscription. Is the hon. member serious in that? Every
hon. member knows-because we all read the newspapers-that during the campaign in Quebec it was said that a vote for Godbout and Lapointe was a vote for conscription. But the hon. member would have us believe that the people of Canada at large were all wrong, that a vote for Duplessis was a vote for participation in the war, and that that was what was being preached during the last provincial campaign. My hon. friend does not believe seriously that he can make the people of Canada swallow that terrible frog?
Then my hon. friend continues to say that during the by-election in Lotbiniere I was supporting Mr. Francoeur. Yes, I am proud to have done so. But the hon. member forgot to say, as everyone who knows anything about recent events must know, that the candidate against Mr. Francoeur was a separatist, a nationalist, an independent, named Mr. Bouchard, who opposed me in the last general election. May I be permitted to say that he was a separatist, an anti-participationist, an anti-war candidate in Quebec East. A Conservative candidate had been selected on the day my good friend Doctor Manion came to address the electors of Quebec. He could not decently endorse Mr. Bouchard, and, as a result, spoke for the other gentleman. But that other gentleman did not open committee rooms, and withdrew two days before polling, asking his friends to vote for the separatist Bouchard. That is the sort of gentleman with whom my hon. friend is associated in Quebec. No wonder he is alone in the House of Commons!
I am not saying anything against Conservatives in the province of Quebec. Heaven knows I would not do that, because they voted for us. They were ashamed of those who were opposing us. That is the reason why my hon. friend, alone, of his clan, is here in the house to-night. He is here because there were two Liberals in the field.
No; in the provincial election of which he spoke and at the general election the Conservatives in Quebec did not vote for gentlemen like my hon. friend, who were running in all the sixty-five constituencies, but preferred to vote for the Liberal candidates and for the participation of Canada in this war. They voted for unity within Canada in this time of terrible conflict. I do not wish to lengthen my remarks, because I believe I have said enough to show that in his speech to-night my hon. friend has not done what he should have done as a representative of his province.
We are proud of the part our province is playing in this conflict. We are proud to be associated with Britain. If there is one

The Address-Mr. Lapointe (Quebec East)
thing my fellow countrymen in Quebec are proud of at this time, it is that they are British as well as Canadian. I have tried to do my duty to my province. My colleagues know that they have done their duty.
The only people in Quebec who at the present time are opposed to the war work of this government are the communists. There may be some others, but they are afraid to express their views. The communists are secretly distributing circulars, and they are calling me names. My good friend, the leader of the opposition, referred to that at Charlottetown. They call me Judas Lapointe and all that sort of thing. I do not want to have the communists on my side. They do all this under cover. As the leader of the opposition said, they have sent me many anonymous letters threatening my life and threatening members of my family. But these people are cowards. When a man wants to do that sort of thing, he does not write a letter, he acts. Even if they do their dirty work, I will not mind. I am here to do my duty, and I shall do it. I shall try at all times to counteract all attacks like the one which the hon. member for Gaspe has launched to-night. I disdain that sort of thing. Let me tell him in all sincerity that as long as the people of the province of Quebec will show, as they have done on many occasions during the last three years, that they are with Cardin, Power and myself, I do not care whom the hon. member for Gaspe may be against.
Motion (Mr. Claxton) agreed to on division.
